WEEKLY SHIPPING MARKET REPORT - pg. 1
Week 31 (24th Jul to 31st Jul 2026)
Bulkers
The Capesize “ Attikos” 179/2012 Sungdong, Korea (SS/DD 01/2027,
Scrubber fitted) was committed to undisclosed interests at USD 37,5 mill. By
way of comparison, the two -years-older sister vessel “Nicholas G.S ”
179/2010 Sungdong, Korea (SS 07/2030, DD 02/2028, Scrubber fitted) was
sold a week ago at UD 34,5 mill.
Japanese owners have committed the Kamsarmax “ Mont Fort ” 82/2012
Tsuneishi, Japan (SS/DD 02/2027, Scrubber fitted) to Greek interests at USD
22 mill . Remind you that the one -year-older sister vessel “Key Hunter”
82/2011 Tsuneishi, Japan (SS/DD 12/2027) was sold a couple of months ago
at USD 20,9 mill.
The Panamax “ G. B. Corrado ” 77/2008 Oshima, Japan (SS/DD 03/2028) of
Gestion Maritime was committed to Korean interests at USD 15 mill . For
reference, the “Alexandros Petrakis” 76/2008 Shin Kasado, Japan (SS/DD
06/2026) was sold back in April at USD 13,3 mill.
Keiyo Kisen have committed their Ultramax “ CMB Jordaens ” 63/2019
Tadotsu, Japan (SS 09/2029, DD 08/2027) at USD 35,5 mill. Note that earlier
this month, the one -year-younger “WF Artemis” 63/2020 Iwagi, Japan (SS
04/2030, DD 05/2028) was sold at USD 36,5 mill.
On the Supramax sector, Atlantides Shipping committed their “ Agios
Nektarios I” 56/2010 Jiangsu, China (SS 08/2030, DD 11/2028) at USD 13,3
mill.

Week 31 (24th Jul to 31st Jul 2026)
Capesize
Iron ore rates on the West Australia to China route showed a firmer tone,
with Port Hedland and Dampier to Qingdao fixtures settling between USD
11.15/12.50 fio. In the Atlantic, Tubarao and Itaguai departures to Qingdao,
including West Africa options, sec ured between USD 32.10/33.75 fio, while
a long-haul run from Port Cartier achieved USD 46.70 fio. Out of South Africa,
a Saldanha Bay trip to Qingdao fetched USD 24.12 fio.
Kamsarmax / Panamax
In the Pacific, Australian rounds with redelivery in China, South Korea, India
and South East Asia fetched between USD 11,750/19,000 pd, alongside a
long-haul trip from Continent via Australia to South Korea fixing at USD
34,400 pd. NoPac  trips with Singapore/Japan, Far East and India options
settled between USD 14,750/18,250 pd. Indonesian coal runs to China, India,
Japan and local ranges achieved USD 11,100/18,000 pd, while a North China
trip to South East Asia made USD 10,000 pd. From E ast Coast India, West
Coast India and South East Asia, trips via ECSA and South Africa to India and
Far East destinations obtained USD 16,000/21,000 pd and USD 19,000 pd
respectively. In the Atlantic, Continent trips via USEC to India and South East
Asia reached between USD 33,000/34,000 pd, while an intra -Continent run
via Narvik made USD 22,000 pd.
Ultramax / Supramax
In the Pacific, trips from North China via Indonesia to East Coast India fixed
at USD 18,000 pd, while a run to the Persian Gulf achieved USD 25,500 pd
and a trip from Singapore to China settled at USD 15,500 pd. From East
Australia, a trip to South East Asia fetched USD 22,000 pd plus USD 345,000
ballast bonus. Out of India, coastal and local round trips, including runs via

Handymax / Handysize
Activity in the Handysize segment remained subdued for another week, with
limited fixtures reported. In the Atlantic, an alumina run from the Caribbean
to Continent fixed at USD 16,500 pd, while a NCSA trip to ECSA range fetched
USD 15,200 pd. Out of Conti nent, a transatlantic grain run to NCSA settled
at USD 9,500 pd, whereas a West Med trip via Safi to West Africa achieved
USD 15,500 pd.

Iron ore rates on the West Australia to China route strengthened, with Port
Hedland and Dampier to Qingdao fixtures settling between USD 15.00/16.30
fio. In the Atlantic, Tubarao departures to Qingdao, including West Africa
options, fetched between USD 34. 25/36.10 fio, while a Boffa run to Yantai
and Longkou reached USD 36.80 fio. Transatlantic activity saw a Tubarao run
to Rotterdam fixing at USD 15.50 fio.
Kamsarmax / Panamax
In the Pacific, Australian rounds with redelivery in China, Japan, Taiwan,
India and South East Asia fetched between USD 16,500/21,000 pd. NoPac
trips with Singapore/Japan and South East Asia options settled between USD
16,250/17,500 pd, while a North America West Coast run to Malaysia made
USD 15,000 pd.

newbuilding vessel fixed for a longer 22 to 24 months period at USD 19,500
pd.

Out of India and the Persian Gulf, coastal and regional runs from West Coast
India to East Coast India settled between USD 19,000/21,000 pd, while a
long-haul trip via South Africa to China made USD 17,500 pd and a PG trip to
ECSA fixed at USD 13,000 pd. O ut of South Africa, coal trips to Far East and
China options secured between USD 18,500/24,500 pd, alongside ballast
bonuses from USD 185,000 to USD 245,000. In the Atlantic, an ECSA grain
run to Singapore/Japan range achieved USD 29,000 pd, while a West M ed
trip via Continent to India obtained USD 24,000 pd. On period, an Ultramax
fixed for 5 to 7 months duration at USD 21,000 pd with Atlantic redelivery.

options, secured between USD 32. 00/34.30 fio. Further East, runs from
Gladstone and HPCT to East Coast India settled at USD 20.40 fio and USD

settled between USD 15,000/19,500 pd. Indonesian coal runs from South

Hay Point–Paradip traced the same path, closing at USD 20.50/mt. The Indonesian thermal coal trade was softer overall, Samarinda–Guangzhou easing to USD 8.75/mt from USD 8.90/mt a week earlier.Fresh Pacific fixtures stayed limited, with charterers maintaining pressure on owners. Bunker prices were volatile but broadly softer.

PRODUCT TANKER MARKETCLEANHandies Cross-MedA confusing week, with rates exploding over the first few days — a WS 275 was even seen on a cross-Italy run — before being swiftly brought back under control by a unit over 20 years old fixing a handful of points below the market, which charterers then used as a reference to keep rates in check. The week closed at around WS 225.Flexies ex MedA busy week across both this segment and the intermediates/small sizes, with most of the well-approved tonnage taken up and fixing windows pushed further forward.
The main challenge for the week ahead will be to see whether the handies begin to threaten the competitiveness of the flexies once again.Intermediates / SmallActivity was equally busy here, with the bulk of the well-approved tonnage absorbed and fixing windows likewise pushed further forward. Tonnage suitable for Italian cabotage is more than scarce.
DIRTYHandiesThe week opened with a tight tonnage list and a number of replacements, which helped owners to keep rates firming up to around WS 355.MRsTonnage in the Mediterranean is tighter than usual, as some units are employed on time charter or are undergoing drydocking, whilst those remaining open continue to assist the handies in covering smaller cargoes. 45,000 mt cross-Mediterranean is assessed at around WS 270.

SALE & PURCHASE 12NEWBUILDING ORDERS Newbuilding activity remained healthy this week, with contracting led by strong demand across the container and dry bulk sectors, while fresh orders were also reported for crude and product tankers, as well as a PCTC. Container activity was dominated by feeder and mid-sized vessels, whereas the dry bulk market saw a series of Ultramax orders alongside larger Newcastlemax commitments.In the dry bulk sector, Turkish owner Aruna Shipping reportedly placed an order for 6x 64,500 dwt Ultramax bulk carriers at Yangzhou Guoyu Shipbuilding, with each vessel valued at approximately USD 35 million and deliveries scheduled between mid-2028 and late-2030. The contract also includes options for four additional units. Greek owner W Marine is also understood to have booked 3x 64,800 dwt Ultramaxes at Jiangsu Dajin Heavy Industry for around USD 33.5 million each, with deliveries throughout 2028. Elsewhere, Greek owner JME Navigation reportedly contracted 1x 64,000 dwt Ultramax at New Dayang
Shipbuilding for approximately USD 35 million, while Cape Shipping S.A. is understood to have confirmed an order for 3x 181,000 dwt Capesize bulk carriers at Hengli Heavy Industry, priced at around USD 76 million each for delivery in late 2027.Tanker ordering also remained active. South Korean owner Pan Ocean reportedly returned to Qingdao Beihai for 2x 319,000 dwt VLCCs, with each vessel valued at approximately USD 122 million. The ammonia-ready vessels are scheduled for delivery in 2030.

With Hormuz functioning again — fourteen commodity vessels transited on Wednesday — owners at last have a working exit route, and the tone turned quietly constructive despite mixed freight, the Baltic Dry Index recovering to 2,673 after a
four-week low.Rankings held steady across the sub-continent. Bangladesh led at USD 445–450 per LDT; the 29 July tide window opened, delivering the first meaningful beachings at Chattogram since the floods, though firmer sentiment has yet to reach vessel pricing and appetite still favours bulkers and clean-history units over discounted tanker tonnage.
India firmed to USD 422–427 per LDT, Alang's plate crossing USD 400 and two yards proposed for the EU List, widening its compliance advantage. Pakistan held USD 443–448 per LDT with plate near USD 714 per tonne, yet Gadani reported no new candidates for a second week. Turkey remained uncompetitive at USD 262–264 per LDT.

Its waters are shared by Russia and Ukraine as well as Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania and Turkey.Ukraine turns to alternative grain export routes, counts losses as Russia blocks ports Alternative grain export routes from Ukraine will reach required capacity at the end of August at the earliest, its agriculture minister said, warning they would cover only half of volumes handled by Black Sea ports disrupted by Russian attacks. Russia has intensified missile and drone attacks on foreign-flagged civilian vessels in the southern Odesa port hub, which handles most of Ukraine's grain shipments. The Capesize market advanced strongly over the week, building on the late-July recovery as typhoon-related concerns and robust iron ore demand tightened tonnage supply across both basins. Rates surged through midweek before steadying, closing markedly higher on all major iron ore routes.The Pacific led the rally. The Western Australia–Qingdao route (170,000 mt iron ore) jumped USD 1.35/wmt to USD 14.35/wmt on 3 August as an approaching typhoon expected to affect central China raised vessel-delay concerns, with a rising number of mining majors seeking prompt tonnage. Momentum accelerated to USD 15.00/wmt on 4 August and a weekly high of USD 16.20/wmt on 5 August, driven by typhoon-induced scheduling inefficiencies and a shrinking fleet around the tight laycan window. The route then eased 30 cents/wmt
to USD 15.90/wmt on 6 August and held there on 7 August as activity turned rangebound, for a net weekly gain of USD 1.55/wmt.The Atlantic firmed in tandem. The Tubarao–Qingdao route climbed from USD 34.60/wmt on 3 August to USD 36.10/wmt on 5 August amid a flurry of Brazil-to-Qingdao fixtures for early-September loading dates and firmer freight derivative (FFA) values.

The Asia-Pacific Panamax market firmed over the week on largely sentiment-driven support, despite choppy day-to-day movements. After a slow start on Monday 3 August, rates advanced as a strengthening east coast South America market, rising freight derivative values and an approaching typhoon (Dolphin) tightened Pacific tonnage and left owners reluctant to discount. lengthy Indonesian tonnage list and lacklustre fresh cargo replenishment tempered gains. Indian Ocean Supramax and Ultramax sentiment stayed under pressure over 3–7 August, as insufficient demand, a lack of outbound activity from the Indian coasts and limited iron ore movement kept a lid on rates. Many participants adopted a wait-and-watch approach amid geopolitical uncertainty, while bunker prices swung sharply through the week.
Out of the Persian Gulf, the limestone trade softened after a brief mid-week lift. Freight to move 50,000 mt of limestone from Mina Saqr to Paradip on the east coast of India eased to USD 16.85/mt by 7 August, from USD 17.10/mt on 3 August, having firmed to USD 17.25/mt on 4 August before retreating. Fixing information remained scant to muted throughout.From South Africa, the coal trade was
choppy but broadly rangebound amid soft sentiment and thin activity. Freight to carry 50,000 mt of coal from Richards Bay Coal Terminal to Port Qasim slipped to USD 21.90/mt on 7 August, from USD 22/mt on 3 August, fluctuating within a USD 21.80–22.25/mt band. Fresh enquiry emerged late in the week, with a 60,000 mt (plus/minus 10%) manganese ore stem from Port Elizabeth/Coega to China worked for 20–23 August laycan.

MARKET REPORT –WEEK 32/2026
SALE & PURCHASE 14
DEMOLITION SALESAppetite turned firmly basin-wide this week, even as no basin sale was reported. The dominant headwind remained freight: the Baltic Dry Index rose for four sessions to 3,063, crossing 3,000 for the first time since early June, with Capesize earnings up more than twenty per cent on the week — firm rates that keep ageing tonnage trading rather than heading to the beach.
A temporary, conditional Hormuz corridor and softer crude near USD 83 framed the backdrop.Rankings held steady across the sub-continent. Bangladesh led at USD 445–450 per LDT, its 29 July tide window clearing the flood-era backlog on schedule and anchorage rebuilding towards the 12 August tides; local plate eased while vessel indications held. India stayed at USD 422–427 per
LDT, Alang buyers actively hunting tonnage after losing candidates to rivals, plate firming above USD 411 per tonne with the two-yard EU List proposal still pending.

COMMODITY NEWS –DRY BULKAluminium supply shock revives long-idled Western smeltersThe supply shock caused by the Iran war is sparking old Western aluminium smelters back into life. The restarts are laden with political significance for Washington and Brussels, both equally desperate to reduce import dependency on a metal that is ubiquitous across a diverse range of industrial sectors. Morgan Stanley expects smaller 2026 deficit for aluminiumMorgan Stanley expects aluminium supply deficit to fall in 2026, and said the market is likely to move into a surplus from 2027. The bank now forecasts a smaller aluminum deficit of 1.1 million tons in 2026 versus the previous forecast of 1.8 million tons.China's aluminium wire exports set to slow as tax-driven arbitrage window closesAn unusual surge in China's exports of aluminium stranded wire looks set to unwind, industry sources say, as falling global aluminium prices erode the profitability of a trade that flourished during the supply shock triggered by the Iran war. Aluminium buyers across Asia and other emerging markets have been importing stranded wire from China to remelt into ingots or process into rods and alloys, while traders and Chinese producers have capitalised on a tax advantage and fears of supply shortages after the Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged aluminium facilities in the Gulf, which accounts for about 9% of global supply.China buys more US soybean cargoes toward 25 million-ton goal                                                                                                              China bought at least five more cargoes of U.S. soybeans overnight, traders said on Wednesday, as Beijing steps up purchases to meet a White House-announced target of 25 million metric tons of U.S. beans

Sentiment across the Indian Ocean was mixed and thinly traded, with owners holding firm ideas on the back of weather-related delays in the wider Pacific (typhoon Bavi) and rising bunker prices.Out of the Persian Gulf, limestone demand underpinned a modest firming despite scant fixing. The benchmark 50,000 mt Mina Saqr–Paradip run eased to USD 15.85/mt on 7 July before recovering
steadily to USD 16.20/mt by 10 July, up from USD 15.95/mt at the week's open. An Indian steel producer was linked to a 50,000 mt limestone stem from Salalah to Paradip/Haldia for 20–25 July laycan.From South Africa, coal fixing stayed muted. The 50,000 mt Richards Bay–Port Qasim benchmark climbed to a mid-week high of USD 21.95/mt on 8 July
before slipping to USD 21.40/mt on 10 July, net softer on the week. A charterer sought 55,000 mt from Richards Bay to Pakistan International Bulk Terminal for 21–30 July laycan.Activity on the west coast of India remained subdued amid the monsoon season and a lack of iron ore movement.

The recycling market stalled this week as two pressures converged. The renewed Middle East conflict lifted oil prices, reviving owner hesitation and suspending the Gulf exit queue; declining Hormuz transits deferred tonnage rather than cancelling it. No sales were reported across any sub-continent destination.
At Chattogram, persistent monsoon flooding halted yard work, thinning cash buyer demand; no trading occurred late in the week. Bangladesh nonetheless topped the rankings on a softening tone at USD 455–460 per LDT for dry bulk. Pakistan held steady at Gadani (USD 443–448 per LDT), the rupee firm near 278.
Alang remained the basin's lowest-priced but steady destination at USD 418–423 per LDT, with plate firming and over 110 vessels awaiting delivery. Aliaga stayed structurally uncompetitive and softening at USD 266–268 per LDT.

In Jan-Jul 2026, however, global crude oil loadings declined by -6.1% y-o-y to 1,190.6 mln tonnes, excluding all cabotage trade, according to vessels tracking data from LSEG. Exports from the Arabian Gulf plunged by -30.8% y-o-y to 351.8 mln t in Jan-Jul 2026, and accounted for 29.5% of global seaborne crude trade, down sharply from the historical norm of about 40%, reflecting the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf. Exports from Russian ports (including oil of Kazakh origin) increased by +7.1% y-o-y to 141.8 mln t in Jan-Jul 2026, or 11.9% of global trade. From South America, exports surged by +33.1% y-o-y to 162.9 mln t. From the USA, exports increased by +17.1% y-o-y to 120.9 mln t in Jan-Jul 2026. From West Africa, exports decreased by -10.4% y-o-y to 91.0 mln t. From ASEAN exports rose by +13.9% y-o-y to 70.5 mln t in Jan-Jul 2026 (this inevitably includes trans-shipped Iranian and Russian cargoes). In terms of demand (measured by arrival at discharge ports), the top single-country seaborne importer of crude oil in Jan-Jul 2026 was China, accounting for 19.5% of global trade. Pacific Panamax sentiment strengthened over the week to 14 August, the Asia-Pacific market drawing support from a firming East Coast South America market, tighter prompt tonnage and lingering weather delays. Owners maintained firm fixing ideas throughout, while charterers moved closer to offer levels to secure vessels with firm itineraries. Activity thinned markedly by Friday, with both sides retreating to the sidelines.
Australian coal led the gains. The Hay Point/Paradip metallurgical coal assessment (75,000 mt) rose from USD 20.80/mt on 7 August to USD 21.60/mt, and Hay Point/Qingdao from USD 18.35/mt to USD 19.45/mt. An Indian steel producer fixed Hay Point/Visakhapatnam at USD 23.05/mt for 10–19 September laycan and at USD 23.25/mt for 15–24 September, while Hay Point/Paradip was reported fixed at USD 21.15/mt for 1–10 September.
Indonesian rounds also firmed, Samarinda/Guangzhou (65,000 mt) gaining to USD 9.85/mt and Banjarmasin/Krishnapatnam and Banjarmasin/Mundra reaching USD 12.20/mt and USD 13.60/mt respectively. Richards Bay/Paradip closed at USD 20.40/mt.Brokers cautioned that the Pacific may have reached a ceiling, with tonnage expected to build as weather-delayed vessels open.

Pacific Basin Supramax and Ultramax sentiment improved modestly over 10–14 August, although trading remained thin throughout. The week opened on a relatively stable but subdued footing, with owners and charterers largely sidelined amid volatile bunker prices, while a public holiday early in the week further curtailed exchanges. From mid-week cargo replenishment picked up and typhoon-related delays tightened prompt tonnage supply in the Far East, lending a
firmer tone to spot rates and to prompt time-charter fixtures, leaving the near-term outlook constructive.On the Indonesia–China thermal coal trade, freight to move 55,000 mt from East Kalimantan to Guangzhou gained 30 cents week on week to USD 12.15/mt, with a Taboneo/Fangcheng–Jingtang stem reported fixed at USD 13/mt. Indonesia–India business was flatter: South Kalimantan–Paradip eased 5 cents to USD 15.75/mt and Navlakhi closed unchanged at USD 19.45/mt,
despite a Muara Berau–Navlakhi fixture at USD 18.20/mt for late-August laycan.Handies underperformed. Australian alumina rates fell sharply, Gladstone–Lianyungang (30,000 mt) shedding USD 1.90 to USD 33.70/mt and Bunbury/Kwinana–Lianyungang USD 2.00 to USD 31.80/mt, as fresh enquiry dried up despite owners' resistance and East China weather delays.

SALE & PURCHASE 12NEWBUILDING ORDERS Newbuilding activity remained strong this week, with contracting spread across the dry bulk, tanker and container sectors. In the dry bulk sector, Chinese owner COSCO Shipping Development reportedly placed an order for 12x 212,000 dwt bulk carriers at Nantong Xiangyu and Shanghai Waigaoqiao, priced at approximately USD 78 million each, with deliveries scheduled between 2028 and 2032. The vessels will be conventionally fuelled. Elsewhere, Goldenport Ship- management reportedly ordered 2x 63,500 dwt bulk carriers at Nantong Xiangyu for around USD 30.5 million each, with deliveries in 2029, bringing the owner's total order for the series to four vessels. Turkish owner Aqmaris is understood to have contracted 2x 64,500 dwt Ultramax bulk carriers at Wuhu Shipyard, for delivery in 2028. Uni-Asia Finance also contracted 1x 40,000 dwt bulk carrier at Nihon Shipyard/Imabari for delivery in 2030.
Tanker ordering was also active.

Tanker ordering was also active. Turkish owner Ditas Deniz Isletmeciligi reportedly placed an order for 2x 157,000 dwt crude oil tankers at DH Shipbuilding, priced at around USD 92.3 million each, with deliveries scheduled for September and December 2029. Greek owner Evalend Shipping also contracted 4x 73,500 dwt tankers at Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, priced at approximately USD 55 million each, with deliveries from March to September 2028. In the VLCC segment, YZJ Maritime is understood to have contracted 4x 306,000 dwt VLCCs at Jiangsu New Hantong for approximately USD 125 million each, with deliveries in September 2029, bringing the owner's total order at the yard to eight vessels. Minsheng Financial Leasing also reportedly contracted 5x 49,900 dwt tankers at Guangzhou Shipyard International for delivery in March 2028. The vessels are to be chartered to Shell International, with a probable purchase option for Shell at a later date; with a similar arrangement, Shell now has 11 vessels of this type on order in China.
In the container segment, Taiwanese liner Wan Hai Lines was particularly active, reportedly ordering 8x 11,000 teu containerships at Shanghai Waigaoqiao for approximately USD 122.5 million each, with deliveries scheduled between December 2028 and September 2030. The vessels are designed to be methanol and LNG dual-fuel ready. Wan Hai also reportedly contracted 4x 6,000 teu containerships at Huangpu Wenchong, with deliveries between March and December 2029, although no contract price has been reported. Chinese owner Zhenghe Mainline is understood to have ordered 6x 4,600 teu containerships at Hengli Heavy Industries for approximately USD 72 million each, with deliveries from March 2029 through June 2030.

SAUDI ARABIA CRUDE OIL EXPORTSAfter a marginal decline in 2024, when global crude oil loadings decreased by -0.2% y-o-y, things picked up in 2025, with full-year volumes increasing by +1.8% y-o-y.In Jan-Jun 2026, however, global crude oil loadings declined by -6.1% y-o-y to 1,016.4 mln tonnes, excluding all cabotage trade, according to vessels tracking data from LSEG.Exports from the Arabian Gulf plunged by -30.7% y-o-y to 299.7 mln t in Jan-Jun 2026, and accounted for 29.5% of global seaborne crude trade, down sharply from the historical norm of about 40%, reflecting the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf.Exports from Russian ports (including oil of Kazakh origin) edged up by +3.5% y-o-y to 117.1 mln t in Jan-Jun 2026, or 11.5% of global trade.From South America, exports surged by +31.5% y-o-y to 137.6 mln t.From the USA, exports increased by +20.5% y-o-y to 107.3 mln t in Jan-Jun 2026.From West Africa, exports decreased by -10.4% y-o-y to 78.2 mln t.From ASEAN exports jumped by +14.7% y-o-y to 59.8 mln t in Jan-Jun 2026 (this includes trans-shipped Iranian, Russian cargoes).In terms of demand (measured by arrival at discharge ports), the top seaborne importer of crude oil in Jan-Jun 2026 was Mainland China, accounting for 20.5% of global trade.Volumes into China decreased by           -14.2% y-o-y to 209.5 mln t in Jan-Jun 2026, from 244.1 mln t in Jan-Jun

Asia-Pacific Panamax freight rates trended firmer, with the Pacific basin drawing consistent support from a firm East Coast South America (ECSA) market that kept ballasting west an attractive option and underpinned owners' bullish fixing ideas. Elevated tonnage levels and thin cargo replenishment capped momentum, yet vessel delays and port congestion from a recent typhoon tightened prompt availability early in the week. Freight derivative rates firmed at the start but softened from mid-week, while bunker prices spiked early — amid Middle East tensions — before retreating over the final two sessions. Trading thinned towards the week's end as charterers covered prompt requirements and retreated to the
sidelines.Australian coal was cited as the principal driver for Pacific rates. The benchmark run for 75,000 mt (plus/minus 10%) of metallurgical coal from Hay Point to Paradip firmed steadily to USD 21.05/mt by 17 July, from USD 19.85/mt on 13 July, while Hay Point to Qingdao edged up to USD 18.40/mt from USD 17.95/mt. Fixtures underpinned sentiment: Hay Point/Visakhapatnam was reported at USD 20.80/mt, USD 21.50/mt and USD 22/mt across successive laycans, while an Abbot Point/Visakhapatnam stem fixed at USD 20.35/mt late in the week.Further enquiry emerged ex Abbot Point and Gladstone.Out of Indonesia, the Samarinda–
Guangzhou coal trade (65,000 mt) proved choppier, climbing to USD 9.60/mt by 15 July before easing to USD 9.15/mt on 17 July as fresh enquiry dried up. On the Indonesia–India leg, thermal coal from Banjarmasin to Krishnapatnam on India's east coast rose to a mid-week USD 11.60/mt before settling at USD 11.50/mt, with the Mundra run on the west coast at USD 12.75/mt. Several coal stems were worked towards south China and India — including Tanjung Bara, Taboneo and Tanjung Pemancingan liftings — though fresh fixtures remained scarce.Overall, the Pacific closed the week on firm but cooling sentiment, owners resisting discounts against the ballast alternative.

The Black Sea and Mediterranean saw a very complicated week. In Ukraine, a series of attacks struck port infrastructure and vessels, also in Russian waters; Ukrainians claimed to have hit 116 Russian vessels with drones. Rates naturally rose, as underwriters immediately raised Additional War Risk premiums for the area and owners must pay crew bonuses,
among other things. On this alone, handy voyage freights rose at least USD 3/pmt. Some vessels bound to Ukraine to load and discharge cargoes, including fertiliser, anchored outside Ukrainian territorial waters, as some P&I clubs suspended war risk cover for Ukrainian-port voyages. Handy rates for intra-Mediterranean climbed to USD 16,000/day.
Transatlantic trips to US Gulf and ECSA improved, reaching USD 9,000/day for ECSA and USD 11,250 to US Gulf. US Gulf now stands at USD 16,500 for Ultramaxes and USD 15,500/16,000 for Supramaxes. The recycling market remained paused rather than broken this week, with no sales reported across the sub-continent. Two forces restrained tonnage: firmer freight — the Baltic Dry Index closed at 2,944, its highest since 5 June — kept ageing vessels trading, while a reinstated naval blockade of Iranian ports delayed the anticipated Gulf exit queue amid renewed war-risk premiums.Bangladesh topped the rankings but
softened, with dry bulk indications of USD 448–453 per LDT; severe flooding around Chattogram slowed beaching to a near-halt, the next meaningful tide window opening 29 July. Pakistan held steady at USD 443–448 per LDT, Gadani plate flat near USD 700 per ton. India was steady at USD 418–423 per LDT, Alang offering the basin's deepest capacity and strongest compliance profile despite the
weakest price; local plate firmed toward USD 394. Turkey remained structurally uncompetitive at USD 263–265 per LDT, its Aliaga market defined by EU regulation and Basel Convention compliance rather than price.Overall sentiment stayed cautious. Firmer earnings and blockade disruption continue to defer recycling candidates, leaving cash buyers with thin enquiry and yards awaiting dry ground.

The Capesize market staged a broad-based recovery over the week, reversing the previous week's losses as firming freight derivative (FFA) values, a sustained climb in bunker prices and improving tonnage demand lifted rates across all major iron ore routes.The week opened on a soft footing. The Western Australia–Qingdao route (170,000 mt iron ore) slipped a further 80 cents/wmt to USD 11.00/wmt on 20 July, weighed down by ample Pacific tonnage supply, declining FFA values and a thin cargo list. Sentiment turned on 21 July, however, with several participants declaring the market had "bottomed out" as bid levels firmed in both basins.

SALE & PURCHASE 12NEWBUILDING ORDERS Newbuilding activity remained brisk this week, with contracting spread across the dry bulk, tanker, container and gas carrier sectors. Dry bulk ordering was led by a series of very large ore carrier and Newcastlemax contracts, while notable activity also emerged in product tankers, feeder containerships and ammonia-ready gas carriers.In the dry bulk sector, Chinese owner China Merchants Energy Shipping reportedly placed an order for 6x 343,000 dwt VLOCs at China Merchants Heavy Industry, with each vessel priced at approximately USD 121.3 million and scheduled for delivery from March 2029. The vessels will reportedly enter into 25-year time charters with Vale for Brazilian iron ore exports to China. Greek owner Evalend Shipping also returned to the market, booking 3x 211,000 dwt Newcastlemaxes at Tangshan Dajin Offshore Engineering for USD 77.5 million each, with deliveries scheduled for the end of 2029 and an option for one
additional unit. Elsewhere, COSCO Shipping Bulk is understood to have ordered 4x 210,000 dwt Newcastlemaxes at Qingdao Beihai, bringing its orderbook for the design to seven vessels. In the smaller bulk segment, Hong Kong-based Seacon Shipping reportedly contracted 2x 26,700 dwt Handysize bulk carriers at Tsuneishi Zhoushan for USD 33 million each, with deliveries scheduled for 2028 and 2030.Tanker ordering also remained firm. Chinese owner Nanjing Tanker Corporation reportedly booked 4x 50,000 dwt product tankers at Guangzhou Shipyard International, priced at around USD 45.7 million each for delivery during 2028.

Although no official contract price has been confirmed, market sources indicate a value in the region of USD 185–200 million per vessel. Elsewhere, Chinese owner Sinotrans is also understood to have ordered 4x 1,800 teu feeder vessels at China Merchants Qingshan, reportedly priced at USD 31.5 million each for delivery in late 2027. In addition, Indian interests Kamal & Adel reportedly placed an order for 1x 1,710 teu feeder at Chizhou Tianyu Shipbuilding for approximately USD 31.5 million.Elsewhere, Greek owner Capital was particularly active in the gas carrier sector, reportedly placing an order for 8x 93,000 cbm LPG/ammonia carriers at Hengli Heavy Industry, with each vessel valued at around USD 125 million and deliveries scheduled during 2028.

SALE & PURCHASE 14
DEMOLITION SALESThe recycling market remained paused, with no sales reported across the sub-continent, though the balance began to shift. A sharp reversal in freight — the Baltic Dry Index fell over six per cent to a low of 2,671, the Capesize index tumbling to 3,889 — delivered the first genuine nudge of ageing tonnage towards the beach in months. Yet renewed war-risk premiums, as Red Sea attacks opened a second
front and Brent crossed USD 100, continued to complicate the Gulf exit routes.Bangladesh softened to USD 445–450 per LDT; Chattogram operations largely normalised as floodwaters receded, the next meaningful tide window opening 29 July, though a post-arrival vessel sanction sharpened compliance caution, tilting appetite towards bulkers and clean-history units. Pakistan held steady at USD 443–448
per LDT, Gadani plate firming to near USD 714 per tonne amid scarce candidates and a persistent scrap shortage. India firmed to USD 420–425 per LDT, Alang's plate approaching USD 400 and its acceptance of dark-fleet tonnage widening its structural advantage. Turkey stayed uncompetitive at USD 262–264 per LDT.

CHARTERING MARKET AT HAND:
HANDYSIZE AND SUPRAMAX/ULTRAMAX// WEEK 31
Handy/Supra market: pressure persists in USG and ECSA, Continent remains flat,
while the Black Sea faces mounting disruption
The Supramax/Ultramax market continues to
weaken in both the USG and ECSA due to extremely
moderate cargo volumes seen for 1H August. Market
participants attribute the current lull to the traditional
vacation season and expect demand to pick up no
earlier than the end of August. At the moment, rates
are falling across all trades, with most significant
declines reported on transatlantic routes. Note that
the Panamax market is putting additional pressure
on the Ultramax sector, as it currently appears more
attractive to charterers in terms of freight levels. By the
end of the week, spot rates in the north have dropped
by $1.5-2k daily and $1-2/t, while South Atlantic
freight levels have sagged within $0.5k daily and $0.5-
1/t. Thus, rates for shipment of 50,000 t of soybeans
or corn from USG to N.China have inched down to
$64-65/t, while those from USG to Tarragona have
decreased to $39-40/t. Handy rates also continue to
decline, and there are no signs of a slowdown in this
trend yet. Only a few cargoes are available on the
market, while the number of open vessels keeps rising
steadily. However, brokers note a localized shortage
of vessels open for mid-August dates. Over the week,
corresponding rates have decreased by $0.5-1k daily
and $1-1.5/t in both parts of the Atlantic.
In North Europe, the market has stabilized at
last week’s levels for now. The bid/offer gap has
widened, as expectations of market participants differ
significantly. Despite a pickup in Turkey’s demand for
European steel scrap, the number of new spot cargo
offers is currently small in the Continent. At the same

The Mediterranean market remains extremely
difficult to analyze, as it essentially comprises three
completely different segments. The so-called “non-

from EU ports, Turkey, and North Africa is definitely
not showing any growth, as the relevant tonnage list
is quite long, and activity has now stabilized following
a slight upturn in recent weeks. At the same time,
the situation is entirely different in the segment for
shipments from Ukraine. Although firm offers from
local ports have become even scarcer than a week
ago, the lack of vessels willing to call at Ukrainian
ports is forcing traders to accept further significant
increases in rates. At the same time, some shipowners’
demands appear “obstinately high” to traders. In any
case, sporadic deals are still being signed; short-

ideas to come down. Meanwhile, the Yemeni Houthis
have announced the blockade on Saudi shipments in
the Red Sea, with some tankers already forced to turn

WEEK 31 · August 1st, 2026
MARKET OVERVIEW
Daily merchant vessel crossings through the Strait of Hormuz have begun to recover from recent lows,
supported in part by active naval escort operations aimed at safeguarding energy exports. Recent
tracking data highlights a notable uptick in transit volumes, marked by the open departure of Qatar’s first
LNG shipment in several weeks alongside specialised gas carriers navigating with dark transponders.
While security risks in the Persian Gulf remain fluid following recent military exchanges, daily energy
outflows have stabilised near six and a half million barrels. This gradual rebound in cargo activity has been
accompanied by exceptionally high freight valuations, with charterers provisionally committing nearly half
a million dollars per day to secure tankers for upcoming loadings destined for East Asia.
Further west, commercial operators are navigating a fragmented security environment across the Red
Sea, balancing persistent regional threats against urgent supply commitments. Vessels calling at Saudi
Arabia’s western loading facilities continue to approach the area despite ongoing hostility near southern
maritime chokepoints. To mitigate exposure, a growing share of Asian crude buyers is taking delivery at
Egyptian Mediterranean terminals, relying on northern pipelines to transfer Middle Eastern crude away
from active conflict zones.
However, fresh safety concerns have emerged near northern canal approaches following unexplained
security incidents involving gas carriers at Egyptian ports, driving additional tankers to hold position
offshore while waiting for operational clarity.
On the macroeconomic front, global financial markets experienced notable volatility as equity indices
posted sharp single-day declines following central bank decisions to maintain elevated interest rates.
Investor sentiment has been further strained by rising energy costs, with benchmark American crude
climbing toward eighty-five dollars a barrel amid concerns over potential military escalation. Monetary
policymakers remain divided, as persistent inflation pressures above target levels have heightened
expectations of future rate hikes.

text:
Segment Highlights
Capesize: Capesize saw a general softening across major basins this week with limited fresh West
Australian iron ore enquiry. Long-haul Atlantic routes out of Brazil and West Africa also encountered
downside pressure due to lower oil prices and quiet overall demand, with shipowners discounting prompt
tonnage to secure employment. As a result, market returns edged lower across most key routes, bringing
Pacific R/V down to US$31,543 per day, with T/A trips holding a slight gain at US$44,247 per day.
Panamax / Kamsarmax: Panamax market softened over the course of the week as the BPI fell 10% amidst
a seasonal summer lull, driven by a drop in Brazilian grain exports alongside reduced coal shipments from
Indonesia and Australia. Thin Atlantic enquiry forced owners to discount prompt tonnage to secure
employment, which dragged T/A rates down to US$19,625 per day. Meanwhile, a late-week improvement
in NOPAC grain enquiry helped steady the East off recent lows, leaving Pacific R/V at US$14,732 per day.
Supramax / Ultramax: Supramax extended its recent downward trend, weighed down by limited fresh
cargo enquiry, expanding tonnage availability in the NOPAC, and spillover competition from softer
Panamax rates. While the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions retained underlying support due to tighter
local vessel lists, a shortage of cargoes across the USG pushed F/H trips to US$28,221 per day. Sluggish
Asian demand and falling Indonesian coal exports further dampened the Eastern basin, dragging
Pacific/India runs to US$17,355 per day and Indonesian R/V to US$14,118 per day.
Handysize: Handysize market traded largely unchanged this week, driven primarily by vessel positioning
rather than any notable shift in cargo demand as a quiet Pacific basin kept fixing activity subdued. While
the Continent and Mediterranean regions maintained a balanced but quiet tone, the wider Atlantic basin
softened further as a growing tonnage list outpaced incoming cargo volume. This expanding vessel
availability weighed on Atlantic returns, dragging T/A rates down to US$15,965 per day while Inter-Pacific
runs edged up slightly to US$15,233 per day.

TANKERS | BDTI: 2,582 ▲+3.20% (w-o-w)
Shipowners are increasingly redirecting empty tankers toward Egypt’s Mediterranean terminal at Sidi Kerir
to collect Saudi crude, as heightened caution increases over sailing near Houthi-threatened waters in the
southern Red Sea. At least eight VLCCs are scheduled to arrive at the Egyptian port by mid-August, as
Saudi Aramco expands sales along this northern corridor via the Suez-Mediterranean (SUMED) pipeline.
Rising insurance restrictions for Saudi calls have prompted several fleet managers—including South
Korea's Sinokor Group—to load at Sidi Kerir instead. At the same time, a cluster of ten empty Saudi tankers

CONTAINERS
The global container shipping market continued its gradual downward correction this week as the SCFI
index fell to 3,062.95 points, signalling a stabilising adjustment rather than a sharp downturn. Reflecting
this broader trend across major trade lanes, the KCCI index dropped 81 points, to settle at 4,123, as the
initial surge from early summer peak-season shipments continued to taper off. Across the Americas and
South America, spot rates on both the U.S. East and West Coasts dipped further under the weight of
waning peak-season demand and shipper resistance to elevated pricing, though MSC’s new Panama
Canal surcharge underscores the persistent, high-cost operational structure underpinning these routes.
Middle East route demonstrated a clear counter-cyclical rebound, rising for a second consecutive week as
escalating security concerns surrounding the Strait of Hormuz prompted carriers to reintroduce risk
premiums, emergency fuel surcharges, and contingency fees. Looking ahead, while the influx of extra
vessel loaders will likely maintain short-term downward pressure on deep-sea trades, the floor for global
freight levels remains insulated by carrier capacity management—including routine 10% blank sailings—
and ongoing vessel diversions away from the Red Sea.

policy decisions and persistent domestic demand challenges in major consuming regions. Iron ore futures
slipped toward CNY 720 per ton, hitting their lowest valuation since June 2025 as financial losses among

purchasing. This weakness extended directly to the finished steel market, where rebar futures fell to near
CNY 3,010 per ton—their weakest point since October 2025—under the strain of a prolonged real estate
slowdown in China, a sector that typically drives about one-third of national steel consumption.
Market sentiment across bulk metals remained cautious as investors anticipated key policy signals from
Beijing's Politburo meeting, where officials are expected to prioritise current fiscal implementation over
aggressive new stimulus packages, while Australian supply remained plentiful after Western Australia's
Pilbara Ports reported shipping 759.4 million tons of iron ore out of more than 800 million tons of total
cargo handled during the 2025–2026 financial year.

01Tankers
VLCC
Suezmax
Geopolitical tensions continue to fuel the volatility in rates. Houthi attacks are now
starting to restrict movements and transits into the Red Sea. Owners willing to transit
are able to attract healthy premiums over the standard Fuj/East run. USG barrels were
a flash in the pan last week with not many ships actually getting fully fixed.
After yesterday's downward correction it comes as no surprise that we have a lengthy
mystery list this morning, along with more enquiries on the sheet, given the overall
fixing hiatus from charterers the week prior. The uptick in activity will help to stabilise
sentiment, however, there are still 15+ ‘natural’ vessels capable of making both
Guyana and West Africa by 20th August. Owners should remain pragmatic in fixing
Aframax
Rates
their vessels away, particularly as the flow of tonnage remains consistent heading into
the third decade.
North Sea
Market has quietly been covering the 1st half of the month with freight levels
remaining relatively steady. Ballasting has slowed with softer surrounding markets but
is still attractive rather than accepting waiting time. The Suezmax market has softened
which may rekindle charterers' appetite for larger vessels with Aframax activity
potentially coming under pressure. Market looks like it will remain steady/soft through
mid month unless we see a jump in activity.
Mediterranean
Very busy Mediterranean market after the corrections of last week. Rates have found a
floor and are hovering around last-done levels, but the position list is slowly becoming
thinner. Volumes are remaining high as Syria and Sidi are pumping additional volumes
at the moment keeping the market interesting.

16.5-17 and one fixture was reported at low to mid USD 16s. First half September

The Panamax market firmed steadily through the week, with momentum broadening
across both basins and owners increasingly able to hold their ground. In the Atlantic,
the fronthaul grain trade remained the principal driver – a healthy flow of South
American and US Gulf cargoes against a tightening tonnage list kept sentiment
constructive and lifted end-month levels, even against continued charterer resistance.
The Pacific firmed in tandem, underpinned by tight prompt tonnage, a steadier stream
of North Pacific grain alongside Australian and Indonesian coal, and some weather-
related disruption that lent owners additional confidence. Period interest was active
and the bid-offer gap narrowed over the week, though owners continued to price
forward cover with a firm hand and a modest premium on shorter durations. With
cargo replenishment healthy in both basins and the forward curve holding a shallow
backwardation, we enter next week on a constructive footing.
The Supramax and Handymax markets remained relatively stable this week. The US
Gulf continued to see the highest activity, while the Continent/Mediterranean
remained balanced despite limited fresh enquiry. South America softened slightly as
cargo volumes eased, and Asia remained quiet with rates edging lower. Overall, the
market remains steady, although fresh cargo demand will be needed for further
improvement.

Desk Talk
Summer seasonality has brought a broader slowdown in market activity, consistent with the typical
seasonal pattern. Against this backdrop, the Strait of Hormuz picture remains little changed: transits stay
well below pre -crisis levels as markets watch for progress in Iran -Oman talks. Flow is concentrated on
discounted Iraqi crude drawing Asian refiner demand, while Iran -Oman's agreement on new routing
coordinates offers a modest positive signal, though Tehran maintains Washington's stance remains the
key hur dle to reopening. Net effect: continued uncertainty weighing on sentiment, with owners still
pricing elevated risk into asset values.
The tone shifts on the S&P side,  where activity varies by segm ent. Purchase inquiries remain heavily
concentrated in the Supramax segment, which continues to see a high volume of inquiries, particularly
for 15–20-year-old tonnage, followed by Handysize, with buyer appetite in these segments still reluctant
to meet current asking premiums. Capesize stands out as the notable exception, with freight rates and
FFAs trading at elevated levels fueling strong S&P interest and firmer pricing in the sector.
On the tanker side, interest remains strong, though buyers are moving a bit more deliberately, taking
their time to make the "right" decision given the high price levels being asked. VLCCs, Suezmaxes, and
Aframaxes continue to draw considerab le interest, with buyer appetite still reluctant to meet current
premiums outright — though some transactions are concluding at more realistic, although still historically
elevated levels relative to prevailing offer ideas.
Capesize activity saw a Japanese -owned unit change hands this week: the "Orange Tiger" (181,399
DWT, 2011-built at Imabari Saijo) found a new owner at an undisclosed level, understood to be in the
upper USD 30 million bracket.
In the Kamsarmax segment, Velos Dry's clients concluded the sale of the scrubber -fitted "Velos Jasper"
(82,167 DWT, 2012-built at Tsuneishi Tadotsu) at roughly USD 23.5 million.

Crude Tanker Comments
The VLCC market was a mixed bag this week. Early on, the Atlantic market leaned in
favour of charterers. Several failures in the previous week and Chinese vessels
ballasting west saw the position list creep up against limited cargo. However, by mid-
week, Atlantic owners were putting up resistance; Brazil-East held at WS 132 to WS
135, and WAF-East stayed near WS 140. The main driver behind this market sentiment
remains East of Suez. Earlier in the week, routes inside high-risk areas of the AG and
Red Sea saw eye-watering earnings, with rates reaching WS 510 to WS 515. Even safer
loading areas in the GOO, such as Fujairah and MAF, stayed firm at around WS 170.
However, a recent Houthi strike on an oil tanker in the Red Sea highlights just how
uncertain those headline numbers really are. If heightened security risks mean that
these routes are no longer viable for most owners, those high rates will have much
less impact on setting a floor for the Atlantic. Adding to the uncertainty, the market is
also closely watching news of a potential agreement between Iran and Oman
regarding a commercial shipping channel through the Strait of Hormuz, which raises
even more questions about future transit security and regional dynamics. For now,
however, strong Middle East returns continue to give Western owners solid leverage.
For Suezmaxes, the week started with Atlantic sentiment under pressure, as limited
WAFR enquiry allowed tonnage to grow and led TD20 to around WS 217.5. CPC
continued to trade at a high premium, a reflection of the ongoing security concerns
and limited number of owners wanting to call Black Sea. As the week progressed,
Atlantic rates corrected sharply, with eastern ballasters flooding the market and
charterers picking friendly faces off the list.

CPC firmed throughout the week, reaching WS 535 for Med, although reports of
loading suspensions added some uncertainty around the premium pricing. In the USG,
a tightening list and a strong WTI demand into Europe helped rates find a floor at WS
160 after a 30-point drop for TA, with charterers increasingly reaching for tonnage
given the favourable economics. By week’s end, the Atlantic appeared to have found a
bottom, with TD20 at WS 175. Charterers returned to the market once lower rates
stabilised, while CPC received support and continues to trade as a two-tier market.
The Med Aframax market faced pressure this week as ample tonnage continued to
outweigh demand, resulting in steady rate corrections and soft sentiment. While
activity levels improved and the position list gradually tightened, downward pressure
on earnings persisted due to the large vessel overhang. By midweek, stronger enquiry
helped trim the front end of the tonnage list further, leading to signs that rates had
found a floor and raising the possibility of a rebound should activity be sustained.
However, limited fresh business at the end of the week left rates flat, and charterers
can continue to lower them. TD19 ends the week at WS 240.
The North Sea Aframax market began the week showing signs of stability, with rates
appearing to have found a floor. However, sentiment gradually weakened as local
activity remained subdued, the position list grew, and pressure from softer
surrounding markets weighed on fundamentals. Initial support from a firmer US Gulf
market faded as momentum there slowed, further reducing confidence. With limited
enquiry and vessel availability increasing, charterers gained leverage and were
increasingly expected to test rates lower. By the end of the week, the overall tone had
softened, with rates still under pressure. TD7 sits at WS 212 on Friday.

This week in the AG LR2 market has been a “tale of two halves”. It began with a few
failures, taking some of the fledgling energy which started at the back end of last
week. There were then renewed attempts to make Arabian Gulf loadings, but these
deals also failed, which is unsurprising when considering the significant logistical and
safety concerns in play regarding the Strait of Hormuz along with the massive prices
asked in a response to the greater risk and to the tighter position list. In the “new
normal” market of Indian Ocean loadings, rates for STS Oman-East moved up five
points on the week to hit WS 190. USD 5 Mn was one of the early week failures for STS
Oman-West, and this is being retested again now with similar levels being likely in
play. The Red Sea has had a dormant period recently but was retested yesterday, with
USD 3.6 Mn being the new Westbound rate. It is a slight decrease from last done, but
with the dearth of enquiry, a much weaker X-Med Aframax market, and northbound
loading in the Red Sea being the safest option, lower numbers begin to make sense.
AG LR1s spent another week in limbo, fully at the mercy of continued geopolitical
tensions. Most public activity was squeezed into one day, on which several naphtha
stems were covered at WS 195 (and at WS 190). Westbound demand has been more
present this week, with USD 3 Mn publicly agreed for an STS Sohar-UKC run. Short-
haul business has not been particularly active, and freight levels have not been
pushed out into the market, but some strong competition could be expected for these
sorts of runs so that owners can remain in the area as AGW rates firm. All in all, there
is no great sign that the war in the Middle East will conclude soon, so market activity

There has been a total change of pace for the LR market in North Asia this week. There
has been more enquiry for both sizebands, much of it initiated by increased Chinese
exports. Several LR2 stems emerged in the market for Australia- and Westbound runs
and backhauls. So far, rates have been unimpressive; USD 4.75 Mn was reported on
subjects for Korea-UKC, with a Singapore option at USD 950,000, but as more cargoes
emerge, we expect owners to push rates north of these levels. The LR1 sector has also
seen an increase in activity, with Chinese exports featuring strongly. There has been
little reported in terms of fixing numbers, but sentiment is firming, and we could well
see the market tick up next week.
Med MR activity has been very subdued this week, with just five or six stems visible
on the surface. As a result, rates have come under pressure, with the lowest tests
sitting at WS 130 TA, WS 150 UKC, and WS 170 Med. Sentiment remains bearish
heading into the weekend and into next week. A softer USG market is expected to
attract fewer ballasters, which could leave the Med with a better-supplied tonnage
list towards the end of the second decade, adding further downward pressure to
rates.
Handysize activity was limited, too. The West Med has seen the better share of
enquiry, with cargoes continuing to trickle in. Combined with a tight tonnage list, this
has helped keep levels broadly stable at around WS 225 X-Med. Central and East Med

WEEK 28 · JULY 10TH, 2026
MARKET OVERVIEW
The tentative peace agreement in the Middle East has experienced a severe setback, presenting a critical
challenge for agricultural powerhouses in the Southern Hemisphere as their primary planting windows
approach. Following a renewed outbreak of regional airstrikes and vessel interdictions, commercial dry
bulk traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has plummeted to an absolute minimum. The timing is
exceptionally sensitive for major crop exporters like Brazil and Argentina, who rely heavily on the Persian
Gulf for roughly a third of their international urea and finished nitrogen supplies. Ongoing logistical data
indicates that only a handful of empty bulk carriers have entered the Gulf to load fertilizer inputs since the
end of June, a dramatic reduction from historical seasonal averages. This mounting transportation
bottleneck is fuelling intense concerns that shipowner confidence will entirely evaporate, leaving vital crop
nutrients stranded at production hubs just as seasonal demand intensifies.
The collapse of the maritime corridor has abruptly reversed the mid-June pricing correction, triggering a
sharp upward surge across global fertilizer benchmarks. Spot prices for urea have jumped over 6% in the
past week alone, marking the most substantial short-term increase in months and pushing trading values
to their highest levels in weeks. Importers in South America, who had previously deferred raw material
purchases in the first half of the year during the height of the conflict, now find themselves with minimal
coverage ahead of the field cycles. For farm operators, these transport restrictions are compounded by
long-term weather risks related to an exceptionally powerful El Niño pattern. The dual pressure of soaring
nutrient costs and potential yield reductions is forcing a structural shift in agricultural planning, with many
producers actively scaling back nutrient-heavy crops in favour of less intensive alternatives.
At the same time, the broader commercial tanker sector is exhibiting an identical flight to caution, with
major independent operators split on whether to continue navigating the volatile chokepoint. While

At the same time, the broader commercial tanker sector is exhibiting an identical flight to caution, with

anchor major portions of their newly assembled fleets off coastal staging areas near Dubai and Pakistan
rather than entering the Gulf to load new crude stems. As a result, spot chartering rates into the region
have surged by an additional US$50,000 a day in highly illiquid trading, creating a fresh financial barrier
for Middle Eastern export facilities that are already struggling to secure compliant hulls amid the threat of
renewed blockades.

highly constrained vessel supply that pushed average daily returns across all asset sizes above long- term
historical norms. Logistical challenges, increased transit distances, and fuel bunkering complications
triggered by disruptions to the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz significantly tightened capacity, an
issue further magnified by intensive shipyard drydocking schedules for aging tonnage buil t during the
construction rush between 2009 and 2011. Although the second half of the year is anticipated to bring
increased market volatility as these advantages begin to recede, new ship deliveries rise to a 4% pace,
and Chinese steel demand cools, positive market confidence is expected to provide temporary  insulation
against these growing structural challenges.

demand recovery, a gradual easing of tonnage pressure in the Atlantic helped lift T/A rates to US$45,250’s
and EC South America F/H to US$74,200’s a day. Near-term momentum remains highly sensitive to
looming discharge disruptions from Typhoon Maysak in China, leaving Pacific R/V  settling at US$38,125’s.

Brazilian grain exports that effectively absorbed excess tonnage across the South American region. While
a heavy buildup of available prompt vessels capsized gains in the Pacific de spite supportive NOPAC cargo

TANKERS | BDTI: 1,988 ▲+7.11% (w-o-w)
The fragile maritime truce in the Middle East has dramatically disintegrated this week, plunging the tanker
segment into immediate chaos. Following alleged Iranian drone strikes on three commercial ships within
the Strait of Hormuz—including a Qatari LNG—the United States launched retaliatory aerial assaults and
revoked the key oil export waiver that had been established under June's 60 -day memorandum of
understanding. With the Joint Maritime Information Center elevating the commercial shipping threat level
to "severe," regular merchant traffic through the primary chokepoint has ground to an abrupt standstill. In
a frantic response to the looming reimposition of a U.S. naval blockade, Tehran deployed a defensive
flotilla of five supertankers and one Suezmax vessel, rushing roughly 11 million barrels of crude into the Gulf
of Oman over a 24-hour window. This sudden return of intense geopolitical risk sent immediate
shockwaves through the energy pricing structures, causing London’s Brent crude to surge nearly 9% this
week to trade around US$79 a barrel.
This acute instability has introduced profound volatility into the VLCC market, where spot chartering rates
are fluctuating wildly on a minute-by-minute basis. While the physical supply side had been exhibiting a
healthy, tangible recovery due to restarted loadings at Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura terminal alongside
expanded export programs out of Iraq, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates, shipowners must now
entirely re-evaluate their risk-versus-reward profiles for Persian Gulf transits.

flow of fresh inquiries hit with the new waves of geopolitical tensions. The fragile environment marked by
renewed U.S.-Iran airstrikes has prompted market participants to stay cautious and carefully assess future
rate direction. In the Atlantic, 260,000mt WAFR/China climbed to WS168.

Aframax: Middle East Aframax market experienced a decline and faces a lingering soft trend due to an
oversupply of available tonnage and ongoing tensions. In contrast, the Mediterranean market saw an
uptick for strong summer sentiment and upward rate pressure near the WS2 17 mark for Ceyhan/Lavera,
driven by a tight volume for end July cargoes.
LR1 / LR2: Middle East LR2 market saw a drop start of week as stabilising regional conditions chipped away
previously held risk premium, but this quickly bounced after return of geopolitical tensions driving rates to
close at WS360 for Japan trips. Similarly, LR1 climbed to WS359 for TC5 routes at closing.

MEG/E.Africa route, TC17 fell some 100 points to close at WS417 while over on the Atlantic, USG  rounded up
slightly with TC14 to UKC closing at WS250’s mark.

Market Insights
Alang, India: Sentiment weakened further through the week, and local prices continued to drift lower on
thin buying interest. Alang is now clearly the sub-continent's price floor; the gap to Gadani at the steel
plate level has widened to roughly USD 310/t, the largest of the year, with Alang plate slipping to INR 36,700
(~USD 385/t) by 3 July.
Alang's counterweight to weak pricing is regulatory: over 110 yards hold valid Statements of Compliance,
and discussions continue with the European Union over adding three Indian yards to the EU -approved list.
If secured, EU-listing would be a structural re-rating for Indian demand, opening tonnage currently routed
to Aliağa. A steady flow of dark-fleet units also continues to arrive, keeping activity visible despite the
subdued spot tone. When the Gulf exit queue routes post-monsoon, it will split on price and compliance —
and on compliance, Alang leads the basin.
On the currency front, USD/INR retreated from a six-week best near INR94.26 on 25 June to trade around
95.1–95.2, surrendering most of the post-ceasefire recovery even with Brent back at pre-war levels. The
pressure is external, Fed repricing, not domestic fundamentals. June CPI (due mid- month) is expected to
stay benign, and the trade bill should narrow materially on USD 71 oil, so the fundamental backdrop
improves even as the currency waits on Washington.

carrying healthy inventories and show little appetite for fresh units, particularly larger, higher-grade
candidates. At USD 266–288/LDT across segments, the price gap to the sub-continent, measured in the
hundreds, keeps Türkiye out of contention for standard tonnage.
Demand therefore remains regulatory rather than commercial: EU flagged and EU compliance driven
vessels continue to route to Aliaga despite materially lower returns. The lira's slide toward 47 (a record
~46.70) firms Turkish offers only at the margin. The central bank held its policy rate at 37% for a third
meeting, and the June CPI print, the first struck against post war, oil will show whether disinflation can
finally take hold. Of the roughly 200 bulkers preparing to exit the Gulf, Alia ga's share will be set by EU and
Basel compliance requirements, not by price.

COMMODITIES, BUNKERS & RATES
Commodities Focus
In the steel and raw materials market, iron ore fines (Fe 61%) spot prices climbed by US$1.15/MT to settle at
US$99.1 CFR China on 8 July, supported by rising Dalian futures where the September contract hit RMB 747
per ton on 9 July. This upward movement was driven by a wave of market anxiety after employees at
Australia's primary export hub, Port Hedland, threatened to strike, which coincided with fresh Middle
Eastern tensions that are expected to inflate maritime freight rates. Despite these supply risks, physical
trading remains thin and constrained by structural headwinds in China, where blast furnace utilization
rates are holding steady at roughly 91%, but finished steel inventories have swelled to 9.35 million MT as of
June 30—marking a substantial 21.6% increase compared to the same period last year. This massive stock
accumulation, including hot-rolled coil and rebar inventories up by nearly 22% and 29% y-o-y respectively,
has pushed domestic rebar sales into financial losses and left mill margins hovering at a precarious
breakeven level.

In addition, September CPC stems are expected to be released imminently. With rates
reaching astronomical levels, owners capable of trading in the Black Sea are likely to
prioritise CPC cargoes over adjacent markets.
North Sea
The stems through the 2nd decade have been depleted for Aframaxes with some
Suezmax activity and a few relets in the mix. With a limited amount of fixtures the
market has steadily fallen over the last week by around 20 points. US markets are
strengthening and pulling tonnage out of the North Sea, so we may have started to
bottom out, and heading into the 3rd decade date wise we could start to see some
pinch points which will see rates bounce.
Mediterranean
A steady week activity wise so far but rates have been eroded. Natural window
pushing into 3rd decade with a list that has been trimmed but still looks relatively
healthy for charterers. With the issues in the Black Sea, tonnage that wouldn’t
normally look X-Mediterranean is recalibrating. Early West Mediterranean positions
are looking at turning right and heading for the land of opportunity across the pond.

down with Baltic printing USD 35.93 and latest offers in low USD 36 range. Pacific C5
ex West Australia/China saw significant activity yesterday in the basin with three
majors in the market. One fixture was done at USD 15.5 for late August dates and an
East Australian stem fixed in the mid-high USD 31s for early September. Today the
Pacific has also seen a slight dip on paper with Baltic down 2% today. Latest offers are
in the low mid USD 14s for late August and early September. Last fixture concluded a
late August Dampier stem at USD 14.25.
The Panamax market has held a constructive tone through the week, with the index
grinding higher after a brief pause mid-week and both basins now pointing in the
same direction. The Atlantic remains led by the fronthaul, where steady South
American and Black Sea grain programmes together with a thinner list of prompt
North Atlantic tonnage have allowed owners to hold their ideas and to resist on
shorter transatlantic business as well. In the Pacific, sentiment has improved on the
back of a fuller NoPac grain order book and firmer Australian coal demand into North
Asia, with Indonesian volumes providing a steady if less dynamic floor; the gap
between available tonnage and cargo requirement is narrowing and charterers are
having to work harder to cover. Period enquiry is genuinely active across both

Desk Talk
Even with the expected seasonal slowdown we are seeing healthy activity in the S&P market, with
several transactions recorded and ongoing negotiations.
With the Strait of Hormu z tensions continuing to shape  market sentiment. Transits through the St rait
remain near record lows , and viole nce has resurfaced, with further Houthi attac ks on commercial
vessels in Bab  el-Mandeb and U.S. forces striking a container ship that attempted to breach
Washington’s blockade on Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman , u nderscoring the security risk  and ri sk
premium pricing across Gulf routes.
Drybulk sentiment remains firm, led by Capesize gains, but strong across sizes, supported by steady iron
ore and coal demand. Capesize Buyers are still active for vessels around 15 years old and, at the same
time we have recorded a number of recent Kamsarmax sales. The majority of enquiries we are seeing,
however, are concentrated in the geared segment, predominantly modern Handy Bulkers, 15-20 years
old Supramaxes and modern Ultramaxes.
On the tanker side, Suezmax spot rates jumped to an assessed global average of USD 108,500/day (from
USD 81,000/day last week) after a burst of USG activity pulled tonnage away from W.Afi ca and Med.
Activity is al so rotating between segments , VLCCs, quiet last week, are now more active in the US G,
while Suezmax demand is shifting Worldwide.
This is also re flected in the increased purchase enq uiries for VLCC, Suezmax and Afra max tonnage,
although in general, sentiment continues to suggest that Buyers are not yet willing to pay the premium
Sellers are asking. On the product tankers side, Buyers are actively looking for MR tonnage of around 15
years of age and younger.

As mentioned, the Kamsarmax sector has seen particularly strong activity recently, with a n umber of
around 10 years old vessels changing hands. The MEDI POSITANO (ABT 82K DWT, 2015, TSUNEISHI ZOSEN,
SCRUBBER) was sold to Greek Buyers for around USD 32m.

Crude Tanker Comments
The week ends with the VLCC market on firm footing, owing mainly to a large uptick in
activity, most of which has been under the radar. The mystery list is the longest it has
been for a while, with over 30 ships disappearing, but a few deals have come out
which showcase the direction of travel. Rates out of Brazil bottomed on Tuesday, with
WS 129.2 being recorded twice for China-bound voyages on a popular market quote.
Since then, the Atlantic list has continued to contract, and next done looks likely to be
in the mid-to-high WS 130s.
Information ex-USG has been limited, with rates and many deals kept under wraps,
but there has been clear activity, and the list prior 20 September is extremely tight. It
remains somewhat on a knife edge as to whether these deals will fix fully, but with the
Suezmax and Aframax markets also looking firm, rates are expected to continue ticking
up for now. WAFR has been quiet on the surface, with just one deal being reported at
WS 135 on older tonnage, but TD15 can be placed in the low-to-mid WS 140s today, a
few points above the BITR print. East of Suez remains active and continues to edge up.
Overall, the outlook is positive, though rates have only firmed gradually as ships
continue to disappear.
For Suezmaxes, the Atlantic has strengthened throughout this week, with both a
tightening list and high level of activity across the sea boosting rates. Last week ended
with a Brazil-UKC fixture printing at WS 177.5, which put TD20 at the WS 182.5 mark. A
flood of end-August cargoes has pushed TD20 to around WS 230, but this is on the
back of an Angola run which discounts to Nigeria and was done with an elderly ship;

likely topped as owners willing to call CPC have prioritised doing this business and are
willing to ballast ships from further afield to chase the earnings here.
The Mediterranean Aframax market softened through the first half of the week as an
oversupplied tonnage list and limited activity continued to weigh on sentiment. Rates
came under significant pressure on Monday amid minimal demand and a growing
number of available vessels. Although a few ships were absorbed on Tuesday and
support from a stronger US market provided some encouragement, vessel supply still
comfortably exceeded cargo demand. By Wednesday, however, activity in the
Mediterranean had started picking up, helping to reduce some excess tonnage and
suggesting that the market may have hit the floor. TD19 ends the week at WS 225,
bouncing back from Wednesday’s WS 205.
The North Sea Aframax market was under pressure for most of the week, reflecting
weak local fundamentals and an abundance of available tonnage following a very
quiet previous week. Rates gradually softened as charterers capitalised on oversupply,
although there was increasing questioning as to how much further values could fall
given strengthening conditions elsewhere. A busy US Gulf market and rising TD25
activity continued to attract ballasting tonnage westbound, helping support rates. By

from the US market allowing for a steady outlook. TD7 sits at WS 200 on Friday.
Product Tanker Comments
On Monday and Tuesday, there was significant demand for AG LR2s, and with the
position list still very much on the leaner side, large improvements were made. There
have mostly been distillates in play, which moved on considerably from the USD 4 Mn
for a non-approved ship last week to the reliable rumour that USD 6.2 Mn is now on
subs for STS Oman or India-UKC via the Suez Canal. Naphtha has been traded less, but
this has also moved on well, with a 20-point improvement leading to WS 210 being
confirmed for 75,000 T. The vessel list is lean going into next week, so the outlook is
firm from the owners’ side.
AG LR1s had potential this week with a much leaner tonnage list, but the market has
barely moved at all. There has been a lot more activity taking place in the shadows
this week, but those fixtures with full details available have seemingly traded
sideways. Naphtha runs heading east have all been agreed at WS 195 throughout the
week. Westbound rates have not been tested publicly, but an agreement of USD 3.3
Mn could be estimated via Bab el-Mandeb. Red Sea activity has suffered in light of
recent Houthi attacks on Saudi business, so it is no surprise that nothing is moving
East through Bab el-Mandeb. Looking into next week, it would take little fresh
demand to kick the LR1s into a firmer market, but for now, it could remain flat.

significant oversupply of available tonnage weighing on the market. Freight levels

It has been a challenging week for NWE MR owners, with a very slow start and a
significant oversupply of available tonnage weighing on the market. Freight levels
across all NWE routes have remained under pressure, with TC2 now last done at WS
105 and the floor yet to be established. Differentials over TC2 have continued to
narrow, with ARA-Brazil now tested down to WS 150 and ARA-UKC at WS 140. Activity
picked up on Thursday and today, helping to absorb some prompt tonnage from the
market. In addition, with sentiment in the USG firm again, five vessels have ballasted
that way, and more are considering their options. This should begin to disperse some
of the current tonnage surplus in NWE and help to start balance tonnage supply.
Med MR owners also had little luck, having to revise ideas sharply to secure cargoes in
a competitive tonnage space. Levels have therefore corrected across the board, with
last done Med-TA now down 25 points to 37KT x WS 110 on a unit whose last cargo
was palm oil. Short-hauls have also suffered, with UKC and X-Med last tested at WS
137.5 and WS 140, respectively. Whilst a rebound in TC14 has already begun to attract
WAFR and West Med ballasters, the outlook for next week still feels bearish
considering current volumes. What remains is a healthy pool of tonnage, which will of
course see further replenishment over the weekend. The market will eventually reach
a point where earnings cannot justify lower rates; however, charterers have a good
chance of squeezing out a bit more in the near term.
The week began slowly for NWE Handysizes. The few cargoes which did emerge
mostly looked at both 30,000 T and 37,000 T options, as the MR market remained
heavily oversupplied and was more economical. As a result, TC23 started the week at
around WS 220 but has fallen to WS 175.

sense is nevertheless that things have slowed down as hostilities have worsen in the
Middle East. President Trump reimposed a naval blockade on all Iranian ports and
Tehran launched strikes on US infrastructure in the region. Early today, the US began
a fresh round of strikes to continue degrading Iranian capabilities used to attack
commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and any further escalation involving the
Strait of Hormuz or additional sanctions on Iranian exports could quickly tighten
market sentiment  and add further risk premiums. Iran's army also said that it had
launched drone attacks against US positions at Jordan's Azraq base and targeted
weapons and storage facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait. War risk insurance is back in the
melting pot, to the extent it is available, and with that rates reported are not
necessarily comparable like for like. The devil is in the detail as the saying goes.

also been depleted with early tonnage heading out of the area both to US and
Mediterranean with owners looking to lock in longer voyages at high daily returns.
Next natural North Sea stems now in the 28-30 window.
Mediterranean
Who would have said that TD19 will be printed at over WS 300 in the middle of
summer. Expensive Suezmaxes, fuel inquiries and a bit of forward fixing have pushed
rates probably at all-time high for the month of July. Charterer are trying to find viable
solutions while owners from surrounding areas are ready to ballast into the
Mediterranean with the dates pushed slowly even to August.

CHARTERING MARKET AT HAND:
COASTERS AND MINIBULKERS // WEEK 33
Coaster market: charterers partially reversed recent surge in Ukrainian freight
rates, Mediterranean and Baltic face a long list of open vessels
Cargo offer continues to grow on the Black Sea
small-tonnage market in the first  half of August,
which primarily applies to shipments from the
Danube ports of Ukraine and Romania. However, the
share of “non-firm” cargoes is only increasing, with
shippers of Ukrainian grain refusing to accept further
rate upturns. Moreover, they are aggressively driving
rates down. “Most traders push rates down; otherwise,
they postpone sales and shipments, so owners start
to accept slightly lower rates,” a Ukrainian broker
told ISM. Despite a gradual decline in the number of
available vessels (down from 67 to 60 units of 2-12k
dwt), rates from Danube ports have dropped by $2-3/
t over the week. Thus, a couple of deals for shipment
of 5-6,000 t of wheat from Izmail or Reni to Alexandria
or Lebanon have been agreed at $62-63/t compared
with $65-67/t a week ago. Cargo flows from ports in
the EU, Turkiye, Russia, and the eastern Mediterranean
appear relatively stable. For instance, transportation
of 6-7,000 t of wheat from Bulgaria to the Italian
Adriatic still costs mid $20s/t bss 1/1. According to
ISM estimates, the rate growth from Russia has also
stalled. “Actually, there is no market from Russian ports
– most details are undisclosed, and fixtures are off the
market,” a Turkish broker noted. Freights from EU Black
Sea ports, as well as within the Mediterranean Sea,
remain unchanged, while RV TCEs are close to historic
lows as for mid-August.
The Azov Sea market remains non-existent.
Meanwhile, activity keeps steadily growing in the
Caspian Sea, as do corresponding freight rates (up
another $4-8/t this week).
