The Baltic & Continent market appears to have
reached the peak of the “summer lull.” Thus, spot cargo
offer remains extremely limited, while the vessel count
has inched up since last week. Local shipowners are
trying to keep rates stable, but spot deals are often
being signed at lower levels.
The Mediterranean and Black Sea markets remain
hostage to the mutual blockade of shipping between
Russia and Ukraine. Even with a possible further
increase in grain shipments from EU ports (including
those transiting from Ukraine), as well as the recovery
of steel and fertilizer traffic, the total cargo volume –
excluding Ukrainian and Russian exports – will still be
insufficient to push freight rates up.
In North Europe, market participants expect a
gradual recovery in activity starting in early September
– the number of new requests for grain shipments in
September is already on the rise, which should help
shipowners drive rates up. We may also see an influx
of vessels from the western Mediterranean if the local
market remains depressed.

WEEKLY MARKET REPORT
WEEK 33 · August 15th, 2026
MARKET OVERVIEW
The cascading effects of ongoing Middle Eastern maritime disruptions are generating unprecedented
congestion across alternative global trade arteries, most notably along the Panama Canal. With primary
transit corridors through the Persian Gulf and the southern Red Sea heavily constrained, international
operators moving containerised freight, energy, and chemical commodities have increasingly pivoted
toward Pacific-to-Atlantic routings. This has triggered severe logistical bottlenecks, stretching waiting
times for unbooked large-capacity vessels to well over a week. To bypass these extensive delays,
commercial operators are committing historic sums in private queue auctions, highlighted this week by
an eye-catching US$4 million bid by a major container ship to secure immediate northbound transit.
Furthermore, the backlog is due to scheduled maintenance outages and draft restrictions stemming from
El Niño-driven seasonal dry spells, which continue to limit daily throughput and elevate operational
expenses across global supply chains.
At the same time, European energy security is facing acute scrutiny as prolonged conflicts severely
throttle standard LNG exports from the Persian Gulf. With regional storage facilities currently standing at
only 59% of capacity, marking the lowest seasonal buffer recorded in over fifteen years, the continent
faces an increasingly narrow window to accumulate necessary heating and power reserves ahead of
peak winter consumption. The near-total curtailment of output from premier Middle Eastern export
terminals has triggered fierce competition between Asian and European buyers for available Atlantic and
spot cargoes. Moreover, distorted market pricing structures, where immediate summer delivery contracts
have traded at substantial premiums over forward winter deliveries, have actively discouraged
commercial traders from injecting gas into storage facilities, leaving government administrators to weigh
the financial and market risks of state backed purchasing interventions.

uncertainty into international financial markets. Major equity indices retreated from recent highs following
data that revealed notable decelerations in consumer sentiment and retail activity, dampening corporate

water levels at Kaub on the Rhine River plunged to record historical lows, severely restricting barge
capacities and forcing major industrial players to divert cargo to rail and road. Against this backdrop, the
main Baltic Dry Index pulled back after its recent weather-driven surge, dropping about 200 points w-o-w
to close at 2,863 points.
This broader market retreat was largely led by the Capesize segment, where BCI slipped to 4,538 points,
reflecting a 11.5% weekly decline compared to last week’s peak. In contrast, BPI posted a 3% drop over the
week to reach 2,228 points—despite ending its ten-day winning streak on Wednesday. Meanwhile, BSI
showed modest regional resilience by edging up to 1,622 points.

passage of Typhoon Dolphin. However, widening discounts in near-month FFA contracts suggest the
recent spot surge was driven more by immediate positioning mismatches than a structural recovery in
Chinese demand. Reflecting these shifting regional dynamics, spot returns adjusted across key routes,
bringing Pacific r/v down to US$43,250 per day with T/A trips at US$43,550’s.
Panamax / Kamsarmax: Panamax market held a constructive tone this week, supported by tight prompt
North Atlantic tonnage alongside steady South American and Black Sea grain programs. Stronger NOPAC
grain enquiry and firm Australian coal demand further narrowed the Pacific supply-demand gap,
offsetting a late week slowdown in Australian and Indonesian cargo volumes. Reflecting these balanced
fundamentals, spot rates adjusted across key routes, bringing T/A rates to US$21,900’s per day, and
Pacific-India runs up to US$16,880’s per day.
Supramax / Ultramax: Supramax ended on a subdued note, with recovering Far East-bound fronthaul
and transatlantic activity in the West being offset by flat, mixed performance in the East. A steady influx of
long-haul and USG cargoes absorbed local vessel capacity to support Atlantic trading, keeping T/A rates
at US$27,000’s despite softer nearby positions and a widening gap between bids and offers. Meanwhile,
Asian markets experienced muted regional demand and correcting backhauls, though slight upward
adjustments helped lift Pacific r/v to US$15,350’s and Indonesian r/v to US$13,700’s per day.

Saudi Arabia is actively re-establishing loading operations at its Persian Gulf export terminals while
balancing ongoing security threats across both primary regional maritime corridors. Satellite imagery
recently captured a VLCC at the Ju’aymah moorings within the Ras Tanura complex, the first recorded
supertanker at the facility in nearly a month alongside a Suezmax vessel at the nearby sea island terminal.
This activity coincides with Saudi Arabia reporting a July production increase of over 1 million BPD to OPEC,
though total output remains significantly below pre-war baselines. However, tracking flows have grown
exceptionally complex as most ships operate with transponders deactivated. Concurrently, export activity
at the Red Sea port of Yanbu has slowed following Houthi threats, forcing a shift in logistics where
northbound shipments through the Suez Canal and the SUMED pipeline to Sidi Kerir reached 2.2 million BPD
last week, effectively replacing the more dangerous southern route through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
With security concerns intensifying, total commercial transits through the Strait of Hormuz have plunged
to just 5 to 10 vessels daily far below the pre-war norm of roughly 140 ships—confirming Tehran's de facto
operational influence over the chokepoints. In response to these persistent vulnerabilities, Western and
regional planners are advancing strategic infrastructure alternatives designed to bypass both the Strait of

With security concerns intensifying, total commercial transits through the Strait of Hormuz have plunged
to just 5 to 10 vessels daily far below the pre-war norm of roughly 140 ships—confirming Tehran's de facto
operational influence over the chokepoints. In response to these persistent vulnerabilities, Western and
regional planners are advancing strategic infrastructure alternatives designed to bypass both the Strait of
Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The newly announced US$5 billion MERA Oil consortium is finalising
a site for a 200,000 BPD refinery and deepwater export hub outside the Persian Gulf on the Gulf of Oman or
Arabian Sea, targeted for completion by late 2029. This project aligns with a broader wartime redesign of
the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) anchored in Oman, as well as proposals for
cross-peninsula land routes toward the Mediterranean.
Segment Highlights
VLCC: Middle East market continues to see surging rates, as Far East charterers rush to secure limited
tonnage amid high war risk insurance premiums. Rates remain elevated with persistent regional transit
risks, with WAFR/China sits around WS140’s.
Suezmax: West African faces persistent bearish pressure as an influx of ballast vessels and returning
Atlantic tonnage maintain a supply overhang against limited spot cargo growth. WAFR/China trips close
around WS185. However, a tightening tonnage-to-cargo ratio and the imminent release of September CPC
stems could stem further rate erosion.
Aframax: MEG is set to maintain a firm tone as a surge in VLCC rates prompts charterers to quickly secure
tonnage, tightening local supply. The Med market faces rate erosion as a healthy position list and Black
Sea tonnage push surplus vessels toward cross-Med voyages closing around WS210.
LR1 / LR2: MEG LR2 market closed strong as prolonged geopolitical risks and expanding STS operations
between the Persian Gulf and Sohar continue to absorb local tonnage. Rates remain well-supported this
with tight vessel availability with TC1 closing at WS517. LR1 rates on the other hand, did not see much
activity with MEG/Japan TC5 closing lower at WS533.

Gaddani, Pakistan: Gadani maintained a firm footing this week, with local recyclers continuing to show
strong appetite for additional tonnage amid robust domestic demand. Offered prices have seen a sudden
spike, driven by a combination of taxation-related considerations, the renewed HKC certification process,
and increasingly aggressive buying from a handful of recyclers eager to secure tonnage. The strength in
ship-recycling prices is particularly notable considering that prime-quality HRC (Hot Rolled Coil) is
currently being imported at around US$560/ton, which may ultimately limit the sustainability of the
present upward momentum.
While local recyclers and steel re-rollers continue to navigate evolving tax and compliance measures,
most notably the revenue authorities’ recent introduction of an electricity consumption based sales tax for
the domestic steel sector, underlying market sentiment has refused to waver.
A major catalyst behind this persistent purchasing appetite is the drastic reduction in overland steel and
scrap imports from neighbouring Iran, which has created an acute structural shortage of meltable
material across the country. Accordingly, domestic steel mills are leaning far more heavily on
shipbreakers to provide essential raw feedstock, considerably strengthening yard operators’ willingness to
compete aggressively and actively bid for any available candidate vessels.
This coincides with a welcome easing in national economic pressures. Official data revealed that
Pakistan's headline inflation slowed significantly to 9.2% in July, down from 11.1% in June, primarily driven by
softer housing and transport costs. With the Asian Development Bank maintaining the country's annual
economic growth projection at 3.7%, improving price stability is helping cushion heavy industries against
earlier cost spikes.

with much caution.

deal on subs for STS Vadinar. As always, one never assumes one sees the whole
picture and some quiet fixing could be happening, but the surface level reporting is
where one gets the ‘read’ of the market and this week it reads like horror fiction.
The only potential positive is that ship supply remains balanced. In most other
marketplaces over the years where demand dries up like this, that would only go
hand-in-hand with a very long position list. However, the fleet has largely been
distributed to other corners of the globe, and the Afra segment of course has retained
a lot of the tonnage all year, which has only grown further this week, with at least
another four CPP ships switching over to the Med DPP trade this week as this market
rallied hard and was much more interesting than the CPP alternative.
This positivity can only be described at best as a sleeping giant; only when demand
returns could any improvements be actualised. Cargo throughput from the AG is very
small and will remain this way until refiners and off-takers have total assurance that
vessel traffic will come to lift the oil; this can’t happen until the SoH is free-flowing,
and we are a very long way from that. Trade virtually stopped this week across all
merchant shipping sectors with a massive deterioration from diplomacy to more
attacks on merchant ships, which led to tragic loss of life on a VLCC. Crew willingness
to trade in this dangerous part of the world has been an integral part of freight
negotiations; that has now of course become a lot harder, which throws up another
barrier in this mire. Vessel insurance has lifted a lot too, which is understandable with
one owner informing us yesterday that premia have gone up x5 since last week. A
further reason as to the deathly silence this week is refining issues in Yanbu, which
has led to a 20-day shut down for repairs, but we believe this might have now come to
an end and the hope is that Red Sea exports could resume next week.

The AG LR1 market remains paralysed. The market remains soft as tonnage far
outstrips current demand levels and this can be seen clearly by the few fixtures out in
public. TC5 ex-Sohar dropped to WS 150, a 25-point drop from last week. Westbound
demand has been limited but USD 2.85 Mn had been agreed for a jet cargo Sikka/UKC
via BEM. There has been some off-market activity which has quietly thinned out the
list vs last week, but there is certainly some way to go before we can see this starting
to improve freight levels. We have seen flutters of activity inside the AG, but given
recent escalations, Indian crew are not permitted to transit SoH as ordered by the
Indian government, and other owners are so more cautious of risk levels, so crossings
have taken a downturn. Shipping remains at the mercy of ongoing and seemingly
worsening war conditions.
In the UKC MR markets, it was a missed opportunity for owners this week. TC2 was at
WS 140-145 on Monday and poised for an increase. However, owners fell into the
trap of not seeking out information and taking open market cargoes as gospel. Activity
levels have been more than enough to at least sustain the market at WS 145 but
unfortunately, we close at WS 140 and look soft going into next week. The fixing
window will move out to end-3rd decade, which looks well supplied with decent
tonnage. The USG shows signs of promise, to the detriment of  TC2; however, this will
likely widen the TA-WAF spread.

CHARTERING MARKET AT HAND:
COASTERS AND MINIBULKERS // WEEK 29
Coaster market divergence: frates soar ex Ukraine, while EU and MENA come
under heavier pressure
As expected, the small-tonnage shipping market
has undergone considerable structural shifts as a result
of the escalation of the air and naval conflict between
Russia and Ukraine. Following several Russian attacks
on vessels in the area of the Greater Odessa ports,
shipowners have started refusing en masse to call
at Ukrainian ports . Most subs have not been finally
lifted, and many shipments have been cancelled.
The gap in expectations is extremely wide, as most
charterers are unable to raise rates, while owners
willing to operate from POC demand a very substantial
premium. “Obviously, it’s very risky; besides, we have
to pay a huge crew bonus and an AWRP that is 3-4
times higher,” a local shipowner commented. Freight
rates ex POC have risen by $2.5-4/t over the week. For
instance, the deal for shipment of 6,000 t of wheat
from Chornomorsk to the North Adriatic is discussed
at mid $40s/t, while transportation of 3,000 t of corn
from Odesa to Cyprus is estimated by brokers at mid
$30s/t. Note that the Danube ports are much more
preferable for shipowners, but vessel count has shrunk
even in this area, so rates have added $1-2/t. Speaking
of shipments from Russian ports, charterers who dare
to work on such biz so far manage to curb any rate
upturns thanks to the influx of a huge number of sea-
river vessels from the Azov Sea, where shipping has
effectively come to a standstill. By the end of the week,
freights for shipments from Novorossiysk, Tuapse and
Taman have grown by mere $0.5-1/t. Thus, shipment of
5-6,000 t of steels from Novorossiysk to Marmara costs
$19.5-20/t. Meanwhile, the segment for shipments
from EU ports, TBS, Georgia, Marmara and EMed was
affected by a massive inflow of tonnage, as most non-

MARKET OVERVIEW
The global sectors are monitoring shifting economic indicators out of East Asia, where China’s central
bank is moving to implement stronger counter-cyclical and cross-cyclical measures to bolster its
domestic economy. Following official data showing that second-quarter GDP growth moderated to 4.3%
falling below the national target and marking the softest expansion in several seasons , monetary
authorities have indicated they will deploy a flexible suite of financial tools, including reserve requirement
ratio cuts and reverse repos, to support liquidity. While aggregate financing and new loans for June both
missed initial forecasts, central banking officials characterised credit expansion for the first half of the year
as reasonable, arguing that a combination of loan and bond financing offers a more accurate metric of
capital flowing into the real economy going forward. To counter external speculation regarding currency
management, the bank emphasised that the yuan would continue to fluctuate naturally based on market
forces, even as the country officially emerges from a three-year deflationary cycle with nominal growth
outpacing real expansion.
Simultaneously, the fragile diplomatic detente in the Middle East has collapsed, plunging the Strait of
Hormuz back into a high-intensity conflict and driving global energy benchmarks higher. Following the
official end of the brief maritime ceasefire and the reinstatement of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports,
military forces have significantly widened the scope of their operations. In a major escalation, an unladen
tanker sailing under a Curacao flag was targeted and disabled by military aircraft deep wi thin the Persian
Gulf while attempting to transit toward Iran's primary export terminal at Kharg Island. With regional
authorities warning that the strategic waterway will remain entirely closed to international shipping unless
foreign forces respect their unilateral traffic rules and proposed service fees, local diplomatic channels
have stalled, raising fears of a protracted, destructive standoff.

a structural premium of up to US$15 a barrel to absorb the ongoing geopolitical risk.

conflict, and a packed shipyard drydocking schedule for ageing vessels built during the late 2000s
shipping boom, which helped keep Capesize earnings highly lucrative at over US $30,000 per day.
However, a weaker outlook for the rest of the year persists due to a tight fertiliser supply evidenced by an
8% drop in global shipments following lower Persian Gulf exports coupled with extreme heat threatening
upcoming September harvests. On the trading floor, the benchmark Baltic Dry Index snapped a winning
streak on Friday, dipping 3.53% w-o-w to 2,840 points. Capesize index also slipped 11.9% to 4,097 points at
week’s closing. The Panamax index rose 0.18% to 2,257 points (up from 2,253 points last week), while the
Supramax index climbed 1.41% to reach 1,730 points, its highest level since August 2022.
Segment Highlights
Capesize: Capesize saw firm upward momentum early in the week in the Pacific. This bullish sentiment
quickly spread to long-haul Atlantic routes, with West Africa/China F/H trading at US$76,250’s and T/A trips
rising to US$48,425’s per day, even as a spike in bunker prices and easing post-midweek activity began to
cap the overall advance. Despite a slightly softer, flat tone in the Pacific toward the end of the week, the
concentrated fixture activity successfully pushed Brazil R/V to US$40,875’s per day.
Panamax / Kamsarmax: Panamax held a firm but consolidating tone this week as a concentration of
China-bound fixtures, anticipated U.S. soybean purchases, and typhoon -related schedule delays
successfully eased prompt tonnage pressure across both basins. Robust NOPAC grain demand and
Australian coal flows drew prompt ships south, providing strong support to Pacific R/V  at US$17,525’s and
Indonesian R/V at US$16,250’s per day. Meanwhile, the Atlantic basin maintained steady floor support from
active USG F/H activity, keeping T/A at US$21,200’s per day.

Supramax / Ultramax: Supramax climbed higher in the Atlantic this week, propelled by tight available
vessel supply and firm, consistent cargo demands out of the USG and Mediterranean. This pushed T/A
rates up to US$27,670’s per day and drove F/H routes to a strong US$29,260’s. In the Pacific, basin softened
slightly as reduced coal shipments bound for China and a growing list of available tonnage dragged
Pacific R/V to US$17,700’s per day, though mounting vessel congestion at Indonesian coal ports helped
cushion the decline.
Handysize: Handies remained highly active this week, supported by a healthy mix of spot and short -
period fixtures across both basins, with the Atlantic generating most of the cargo flow. Tonnage circulation
remained steady as consistent grain, coal, fertiliser, and petcoke trades kept vessels moving and provided
reliable short-haul employment opportunities in Asia. This dynamic helped push T/A rates up to
US$16,950’s, while Pacific R/V edged up to US$15,000’s while Inter-Pacific trips settled at US$15,600’s/day.

Market Insights
Alang, India: Alang experienced a modest gain this week, driven by a tightening of immediate inventory.
The flow slowed to a crawl due to a combination of seasonal monsoon disruptions and a backlog of
incoming tonnage waiting further out at sea. With fewer vessels actively beaching and cutting operations
operating at a reduced pace, the localised scarcity of heavy steel plates artificially elevated trading
sentiments.
Beneath the surface of this price correction, the underlying foundation of the market remains soft.
Consumer-level demand for finished steel products is heavily depressed across domestic infrastructure
and manufacturing sectors, keeping rolling mills highly selective and conservative in their buying patterns.
While Alang’s ship recyclers are deeply eager to acquire fresh tonnage to replenish their yards, they are
facing steep uphill battles. Competing recycling destinations across South Asia continue to put forward
aggressive, higher priced bids, leaving Indian yards struggling to secure commercial tonnage at workable
margins.
While the IMF has projected India to lead major economies with a 6.4% GDP growth rate for the fiscal year,
escalating geopolitical shocks are testing local stability. The resurgence of conflict in the Middle East has
triggered a severe global energy spike, driving Brent crude higher and heavily inflating India’s energy
import bill.

Suezmax
We’re in “stop the press” territory now with VLCC rates galloping in all areas in tandem
with the Suez- and Aframax segments. In the Atlantic we saw a stonking WS 197.5
fixture Brazil/China yesterday, up from a WS 182.5 just done a bit earlier! An
unconfirmed report suggests WS 210 has been done West Africa/East, but whether
true or not tallies with the last Brazil rate, if not higher. Fujairah-Oman/East cargoes
have followed suit sniffing on the WS 200 mark or above. Position lists are thinning by
the hour both east and west of Suez so today’s “expensive” fixture might very well
look “cheap” tomorrow. Time and tide wait for no man.
On the one hand we have prompt replacements & 1-5 window cargoes working
Suezmax, VLCC levels also in runaway mode with TD15 fixing circa 260KT x WS 200
Aframax
Rates
and their USG list almost devoid of tonnage within the next 30-day. Thus expectations
of strong West Africa demand to carry the Suezmax market in the 2nd decade could
sustain this spike. On the other, we are fully priced out of the USG market with 2
enquiries withdrawing yesterday & Aframaxes USD 2.5/BBL cheaper, and basis latest
cargo counts ex West Africa we may be down to our final 6 stems in the 1st decade
once present enquiry is cleaned out.
The list has 8 natural options FOC up to the 5th, 4 discharging presently, 3 at disport

should give owners in the 2nd decade, even if 1st decade demand falls off a little

pushovers.
North Sea
The North Sea list has been greatly reduced with vessels heading to the US. The
amount of vessels in ballast to the US so far in August is the largest amount we have
seen in the same period in any previous month. The North Sea market has remained
steady even with the clearing of the list holding around the WS 200 level. Dates are
starting to push towards the end of the month which should see some increase in
activity and itineraries will be important for B/L dates which may allow owners to
chase a slight premium.
Mediterranean
Activity in the Mediterranean has been consistent with a few replacement
requirements also coming into the mix. The US has attracted vessels from the West
Mediterranean along with some compromised vessels has kept the tonnage available
to charterers interesting. Rates have firmed around WS 15 points from last week and
heading to the end August/early September fixing window we may still see some
more firming.

This week markets are showing slight pressure with limited fixing today on Capesize
across all segments, however markets are consistent on C3 Brazil/China with the main
decline seen in Pacific C5. FFAs show slight positive sentiment in the long term
although above average laden to ballast ratio of vessels heading toward the Atlantic
gives a slight bearish outlook in the near future. This week sentiment has had a softer
tone in the Pacific and today saw a decline on paper. Earlier fixing concluded around
and just below the USD 14 range for West Australia/Qingdao. Today, two miners
reported fixing at USD 13.4 yesterday and latest bids are mixed and around USD 13 to
USD 14 for early September laycans. In the Atlantic, levels have remained consistent
however South Brazil and West Africa to China remains subdued with limited bids and
offers reported today. C3 Brazil/China sees bids and offer reported in low USD 36
levels with last done in high USD 34s on C3 for West Africa and another reported in
the USD 37 range on Friday for a Newcastlemax.

levels with last done in high USD 34s on C3 for West Africa and another reported in
the USD 37 range on Friday for a Newcastlemax.
Panamax sentiment has turned more cautious this week, with the index giving back
part of its recent gains and both basins trading with a softer bias. The Pacific has led
the correction: prompt tonnage has accumulated across the North and South while
fresh NoPac grain and Australian and Indo coal enquiry has been slow to absorb it,
leaving charterers in control and the market still in search of a floor. The Atlantic has
held up rather better, with ECSA fronthaul remaining the firmer leg and Continent
tonnage still reasonably tight, although bid/offer have widened and fixing volumes are
thin as charterers wait for the north to settle. Period discussion remains active across
both Kamsarmax and Panamax, but owners are resisting the softer nearby curve and
bids have yet to close the gap, so relatively little is concluding. We would expect a
sideways-to-softer tone into next week, with any recovery contingent on a fresh
injection of grain and coal cargo in the Pacific; in the meantime the Atlantic should
continue to offer owners the better alternative.
Supramax market remained broadly steady, with limited movement across most
regions and only modest gains in the Atlantic. The Continent and Mediterranean
continue to face pressure due to ample tonnage and limited fresh cargo input, while
Rates
the South Atlantic remains more balanced but somewhat positional. In Asia, sentiment
is improving, supported by better activity in NoPac and Southeast Asia, although this
has yet to translate into significant rate gains.
Handy market wise- another subdued session overall, with the Continent and
Mediterranean remaining soft amid limited cargo volumes. The South Atlantic and
USG were broadly stable, with little change in fundamentals. Asia remained the
strongest area, supported by tighter prompt tonnage and steady cargo flow, although
activity remained relatively limited.

Desk Talk
Market sentiment this week continued to be shaped by escalating security risk across two flashpoints .
Hormuz transits stayed near record lows, with attacks continuing, and the Black Sea saw a fresh spike in
hostilities.
On Ta nkers, Suezmax demand remained strong, spanning from the US Gulf , West Africa, the
Mediterranean and now Yanbu, while VLCCs are also seeing active chartering  activity across multiple
loading regions, including inside Hormuz itself.
Ship-to-ship activity off Oman and Fujairah continues to build as exporters find ways to move crude
despite ongoing Strait disruption, and there are early signs that some inner -Gulf export activity is
cautiously resuming, though still limited to risk-tolerant players.
Crucially, market strength is no longer seen as purely a spot -market phenomenon, but FFAs have also
moved up meaningfully, signaling that the market expects elevated earnings, and a substantial Hormuz
risk premium to persist well into next year. This shift in sentiment , from a short -term disruption story to a
structurally longer-term outlook is a key support for asset values, reinforcing Owners' conviction on firm
pricing.
Beyond tankers, attention is also turning to a strengthening El Niño and its potential to disrupt the
Panama Canal later this year, with early restrictions already being announced.
Dry bulk sentiment remains firm, with Capesize rates assessed at USD 40,200/day, supported by rising
Chinese iron ore imports (up to 105.3 million tons in the January-July period from 99.6 million tons a year
earlier) as domestic production declines.
Tanker enquiries this week remained concentrated on larger tonnage, with VLCCs offering prompt
delivery near the AG standing out . On the dry side, enquiries were more evenly distributed across all
segments, with a particular buying interest towards Capesizes.

Crude Tanker Comments
VLCCs had a very strong week. Deferred WAFR cargoes returning to the market and
steady Brazil and USG demand come as prompt VLCC supply is particularly thin in the
Atlantic. The result has been a shift in leverage towards owners; USG-East has climbed
from USD 21 Mn to USD 25 Mn, whilst WAFR-East moved from around WS 148 to WS
220. Brazil has performed very well, too, with Eastbound business moving from WS
200.5 to WS 215. The Brazil-East vs. WAFR-East differential briefly stretched to around
20 points, four times the usual spread, largely due to the strong Suezmax market;
Brazil, meanwhile, remained firmly a VLCC market. Today’s WS 215 suggests that Brazil
charterers now have to compete more for tonnage, reducing the differential.
East of Suez has been equally strong. WS 759 was rumoured for inside AG-East,
Fujairah-East reached WS 220, and Yanbu-East went on subs at WS 345. Demand is on
the rise, and Middle East security concerns support tonne-miles. There are some signs
that owners should keep their expectations in check; later dates, particularly ex-
Fujairah, show more availability, and a USG-China fixture reported at USD 24.4 Mn
failed. For now, though, the balance remains firmly with owners; demand is building,
tonnage is scarce, and the broader tanker markets continue to provide a strong floor.
The Premier League returns this week, and the Suezmax market shares similarities
with a typical league campaign in last-minute substitutions, expensive fees, and points
being put on the board. WAFR continued as it left off, with several late August and
early September cargoes left over from last week and some replacement business
boosting sentiment. Rates jumped from WS 260 to WS 330!

the USG, discouraging ballasting. Still, by the end of the week, owners held the upper

and left room for more rises next week. TD19 sits at WS 257 on Friday.

The North Sea Aframax market remained broadly stable this week despite support
from stronger markets elsewhere. At the beginning, rates held steady as vessels
continued to ballast across the Atlantic. By Tuesday, firming conditions in the
Mediterranean and USG suggested that North Sea levels would become increasingly
difficult to repeat. A pickup in activity then helped maintain rates, although TD7 was
much lower than TD25, encouraging further ballasting. By Thursday, local rates had
surprisingly failed to respond despite the large TD25 premium, with activity still
insufficient to tighten the market significantly. TD7 ends the week at WS 200.
Product Tanker Comments
It was not a very busy week for AG LR2s, but the market nevertheless remains firm. It
is worth noting that much of the week’s activity has been taking place in the shadows,
but either way, there is continued pressure on tonnage supply for what demand is out
there. Westbound fixing has mostly been conducted privately, but USD 6.5 Mn has
been bounced around the market basis UKC via Bab el-Mandeb. Naphtha East runs
have not been thoroughly tested publicly, but freight can be estimated at WS 235 for
TC1. There is little else going on for LR2s, but sentiment is still firm.
There is a much more positive outlook for AG LR1s to close the week; rates have
ticked up when tested, and the tonnage list remains under pressure, with several
vessels disappearing. TC5 jumped from WS 195 to WS 220 midweek but then demand
dialled down. Westbound demand has been patchy, but this business has also firmed
– a USD 300,000  jump on last-done levels to USD 4.2 Mn had been agreed basis UKC
via Bab el-Mandeb, and next-done levels likely sit up at USD 4.5 Mn for the same. Not
much demand has existed outside of Eastbound naphtha and Westbound ULSD and
jet fuel business, but any levels tested are expected to be firmer.

initial softening at the start of the week. Demand has not been overwhelming but has

It was largely an unexciting week for MRs in the region, with rates flat after some
initial softening at the start of the week. Demand has not been overwhelming but has
steadily spread across the week, and the majority has loaded out of WCI. TC17
dropped to WS 275, and this was subsequently repeated several times. The list is still
lean, and there could have been an opportunity for MR rates to bounce back by riding
the coattails of the firming LRs, but this did not materialise. There is little demand
outside of TC12 – latest paying WS 210 – and TC17, but it probably would not take
much to increase the market temperature.
European LR1 activity unexpectedly strengthened due to an influx of available
tonnage, creating chartering opportunities despite softer rates early in the week.
Middle Eastern market strength supported owner sentiment and established a firm
rate floor. LR2s remained tight, but weaker demand limited gains. Strong Middle
Eastern markets should support firmer European freight levels going forward.
It was yet another trying week for Med MR owners, with volumes unable to keep up
with an ever-growing tonnage list. Fundamentally, there should be further corrections
here, but with TA paying 37KT x WS 115, West Med tonnage has opted to ballast
across to the greener grass. A significant fleet remains in the East Med for end-month
dates, which is likely to maintain pressure next week. Med-UKC last tested at 37KT x
WS 140, with X-Med assessed at 37KT x WS 155. Longer hauls have largely remained
untested this week, with WAFR and Brazil assessed at WS 160 and WS 165,
respectively.
Med Handy activity was lacklustre throughout the week, and thus there have been
more corrections. Despite some owners attempting to hold at 30KT x WS 170, others
have succumbed to sustained tonnage competition, and at the time of writing, 30KT x
WS 165 is the consolidated rate.

info@hellenicshippingnews.com
01Tankers
VLCC
Petrobras managed to chip off another 15 and a bit points off their last done
Brazil/East enquiry yesterday, down 51 points from the high in the better part of a
week, and the likelihood is they’ll manage a bit more on their next enquiry as owners
shy away from potential danger in the Middle East and head west. On the other side,
now that both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait are fast becoming a
“no go zone” focus must change to alternative supply from the likes of USG and West
Africa, and punchy Suez- and Aframax rates will encourage economy of scale both
transatlantic and eastbound. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a meeting of
Southeast Asian foreign ministers today that the US is still willing to negotiate an end
to the Iran crisis, but Tehran is not serious about talks. Where there’s a will there’s a
way they say, but where it leads right now is anyone’s guess. One day (hour) at the
time….
Suezmax
Aframax
Rates
Stronger USG Aframax rates are expected to improve the sentiment across the
Atlantic, while limited VLCC availability in West Africa ahead of the 10th prohibits their
crash from disrupting volume in the present window. That said, any disruption to CPC
exports could lead to more tonnage seeking employment in the Atlantic basin & VLCC
rates look like they are on a collision course, and at the very least encourage 2nd
decade charterers to utilise them at higher rates than we have become accustomed to.
Looking ahead, continued tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and growing uncertainty
surrounding Aden transits are encouraging more vessels to ballast West, which may
place some pressure on the Atlantic markets going forward, but demand
fundamentals ex West Africa (12MBBLS 1st decade / 26MBBLS 2nd decade uncovered)
could counterweight this.
North Sea
North Sea and Mediterranean markets have settled down activity wise in the early part
of the week after what had been a very active couple of weeks. The North Sea list

North Sea
North Sea and Mediterranean markets have settled down activity wise in the early part
of the week after what had been a very active couple of weeks. The North Sea list
remains on the thin side but natural dates now pushing into August with the potential
for relets to come back into the frame. The list will be further depleted especially the
early part with tonnage heading off to the very firm US markets. For a Summer market
rates remain strong giving owners very healthy returns.
Mediterranean
Rates in the Mediterranean continue in the high WS 300s with a bit of underground
activity so far this week but slower compared to the chaos of last week. At first look
tonnage list is long however delays in Trieste, vessels ballasting from the Red Sea-East
and potentially ballasting towards USG might keep it more balanced. Returns are too
good for owners to say 'no', if a small discount is required but sentiment remains
strong. Black Sea disruptions are expected to negatively affect the rates if loadings will
get cancelled.

MARKET OVERVIEW
International traders are adopting innovative logistical strategies to bypass mounting bottlenecks and
record-breaking transit costs at the Panama Canal. With drought conditions linked to an intensifying
weather pattern lowering local water reserves and prompting authorities to restrict daily passage
allocations, the cost to secure immediate transit slots for larger gas carriers surged to unprecedented
heights of US$4.6 million. To avoid these exorbitant expenses, major energy corporations are increasingly
deploying cargo transfers off the Pacific entrance near Balboa. Under this model, smaller vessels that
navigate the canal's conventional locks transfer fuel loads directly to larger carriers positioned offshore,
which then commence the transpacific journey to key Asian centers.
In East Asia, the corporate landscape witnessed the historic conclusion to a multi-year debt crisis as
judicial authorities handed down a life sentence to the founder of Evergrande alongside several senior
executives. The landmark ruling follows extensive state investigations into widespread financial
misstatements, unauthorised fundraising, and concealed debt obligations that ultimately precipitated the
group's default and subsequent liquidation. While massive corporate penalties have been levied and
extensive asset seizures ordered, the formal resolution provides a measure of closure for broader markets.
For global maritime, the development marks a defining end to an era of unbridled real estate expansion
that previously fuelled substantial bulk commodity demand, reinforcing a broader transition toward more
measured industrial growth across the region.
Meanwhile, U.S. energy markets are bracing for a temporary tightening of regional feedstock supply just as
domestic processing activity reaches multi-year highs. Refineries operating across the central United
States, which have been running at peak capacity to capitalise on historic distillate margins, face
imminent delivery reductions due to scheduled maintenance across Canadian oil sands facilities next
month. With regional storage hubs in Alberta hovering near historic seasonal lows, the anticipated
curtailment of hundreds of thousands of daily barrels will leave processing plants with minimal buffer
stocks.

Dry bulk market maintained its historically elevated stance, with rate volatility remaining near multi-year
lows as persistent geopolitical disruptions and tight shipyard drydocking schedules continue to restrict
available vessel capacity. While softer Chinese iron ore demand presents an ongoing medium-term
challenge for broader market balance, strong liquidity reserves built over several highly profitable years
provide shipowners with a solid buffer against potential macro headwinds.
On the trading floor, the benchmark Baltic Dry Index fell to 2,841 points, a slight 0.77% weekly decline when
compared against Week 33’s standing. Segment performance showed clear structural divergence
throughout the week, with Capesize rates maintaining a firm presence to help offset downward
momentum in the Panamax sector—which drifted to 2,103 points amid ample tonnage and quieter grain
demand—while the Supramax segment demonstrated steady support near 1,640 points (up from last
week's 1,603 points) on the back of resilient regional trade flows.

Segment Highlights
Capesize: Capesize softened overall this week as C5 rates fell 11.5% due to slower Western Australian iron
ore volumes and the return of open vessel capacity following the resolution of weather disruptions. In
contrast, steady long-haul cargo volumes from Brazil helped maintain stability despite quiet fixture
activity across the wider Atlantic. Reflecting this regional correction, spot earnings moved lower across
most key routes, bringing Pacific r/v down to US$37,250’s with T/A trips at US$40,575 per day.
Panamax / Kamsarmax: Panamax softened this week as spot rates slipped, weighed down by a decline in
Brazilian grain exports alongside a drop in Indonesian coal volumes. Although Australian grain enquiries
helped absorb some regional tonnage, expanding vessel availability in the North Atlantic and a cautious
tone across both basins kept charterers in control and widened the gap between bids and offers.
Consequently, spot returns faced a broad correction across key routes, bringing T/A rates down to
US$19,760’s and Pacific r/v to US$16,200’s per day.
Supramax / Ultramax: Supramax held broadly steady, rising as solid long-haul demand from the USG and
NOPAC helped offset persistent weakness in Southeast Asia. While an influx of North American stems
absorbed vessel capacity and supported the Atlantic, ample tonnage and limited fresh enquiry across the
Continent and Mediterranean continued to cap further upside potential. Reflecting these balanced
regional conditions, spot returns edged slightly higher across major routes, lifting T/A rates to US$27,360’s
and Pacific r/v to US$15,600’s.
Handysize: Handysize saw another subdued session, with the Continent and Mediterranean remaining
soft due to limited cargo volumes while the USG and South Atlantic traded broadly stable. Asia proved to
be the strongest performing region, supported by tighter prompt tonnage availability and steady cargo
flows despite relatively limited fixing activity. Reflecting modest gains across key trades, spot rates moved
upward across the board, lifting T/A rates to US$15,800’s per day with Inter-Pacific routes to US$15,725’s.

VLCC segment is witnessing another historic surge in freight rates as access through the Arabian Gulf
narrows to a trickle. Daily earnings on the benchmark Middle East-to-China route have broken past the
US$500,000 mark, with single-voyage lump-sum fixtures reaching a staggering US$31 million, as
demonstrated by the recent booking of the Mongolia Prosperity. To maintain exports, producers are relying
heavily on shuttle operations, with Saudi Aramco recently loading three tankers at Ras Tanura for prompt
S-T-S transfers off Fujairah. At the same time, major Chinese state shippers like COSCO and CMES have
pulled more than 100 tankers from entering the waterway entirely, choosing instead to collect outside the
chokepoint in Oman and the UAE. This has left global fleet deployment heavily skewed, with 592 empty
tankers currently ballasting across international waters against just 372 actively loaded vessels.
This freight spike reflects a severe deterioration in physical security, marked by seven vessel attacks in the
passage this month alone and the recent halting of the tanker Amara near Qeshm Island. Daily crude
movements through the Strait of Hormuz have fallen to roughly 2 million BPD, down from 4.8 million in July
and representing barely 11% of the 18 million barrels moved daily prior to the conflict. The broader Middle
Eastern export volume has halved to 9.5 million BPD compared to 21 million in 2025, with Iranian shipments
shrinking to 294,000 BPD. With China's refinery throughput inching up 0.3% month-on-month to 12.5 million
BPD —supported by a 25 to 28 million barrel draw on domestic inventories—and the IEA projecting a full-

Segment Highlights
VLCC: After a brief dip, Middle East VLCC rates surged to WS570 as heightened tensions—reignited by the
U.S. decisions—prompted shipowners to aggressively raise quotes. With position lists rapidly thinning on
both sides of Suez, rates across, including Brazil, West Africa, and Fujairah-Oman, are galloping higher in a
fast-moving, owner-favourable market. 260,000mt WAFR/China also saw rates jump to WS209.
Suezmax: West African market surged, propelled by shrinking prompt tonnage, a rush of late-August
stems, and runaway VLCC rates that pushed indices past WS328 for Nigeria/UKC. Rates are poised for
further strength on the back of owner leverage and firm second-decade demand, though dwindling first-
decade stems and being priced out of the USG by cheaper Aframaxes may temper the rally.
Aframax: Aframax are poised to maintain their firm momentum this week as steady Australian regional
crude flows tighten tonnage lists, with owners continuing to demand geopolitical risk premiums. Across
the Mediterranean, rates have gained around 23 points on consistent inquiry and prompt replacement
needs with Ceyhan/Lavera closing WS250, pointing toward further firming as vessels are drawn away
toward the U.S. market into late August and early September.
LR1 / LR2: Middle East LR2 closed lower as renewed tanker attacks in the Strait triggered delays, STS transfer
cancellations, and a sharp drop in fresh cargo inquiries. TC1 MEG/Japan gained momentum closing higher
at WS536. In the LR1 segment, rates also shifted upwards with TC5 seeing gains settling at WS565.

CONTAINERS
The global container shipping market sustained its upward trajectory for a third consecutive week as the
SCFI rose 1.62%, to reach 3,409.63 points. This resilience was fuelled by robust U.S. peak-season demand
extending well past initial expectations, combined with severe typhoons and weather disruptions in
eastern and southern China that pushed vessel waiting times to 87 hours in Shanghai and 36 hours in
Ningbo, sharply restricting effective fleet capacity across transpacific corridors. Pricing also found strong
support in the Middle East—where minimal transit flows through the Strait of Hormuz and concentrated
bottlenecks at alternative hubs like Jeddah have elevated the regional rate floor.

Market Insights
Alang, India: Alang saw a welcome boost in domestic pricing, with local ship steel plate and melting scrap
values strengthened noticeably m-o-m. The common plate price increased from INR 38,400/MT to INR
40,500/MT, a rise of INR 2,100/MT or about 5.5%. Similarly, ship melting scrap prices improved from INR
33,300/MT to INR 34,500/MT, gaining INR 1,200/MT or about 3.6%
.
The month-on-month improvement reflects firmer domestic steel sentiment and stronger recycler appetite, with
the sharper increase in higher-grade 8 ANI material indicating improved demand for reusable ship steel.
Supported by a steady currency exchange rate, providing local buyers with much needed margin relief.
While overall sentiment remains upbeat and end buyers continue to display an active appetite for fresh
tonnage, Alang faces persistent headwinds in the international bidding arena.
Substantial price premiums offered by competing yards in Pakistan and Bangladesh continue to make
conventional dry bulk carriers and container vessels difficult for Indian recyclers to secure. However, Alang
remains uniquely positioned at both ends of the market, serving as the only destination for sanctioned
tonnage, while also attracting highly sophisticated vessels requiring stringent, fully compliant green
recycling standards.

India: Imported containerised shredded scrap strengthened alongside domestic steel to US$395–400/t
CFR, while HMS 80:20 stood near US$340/t CFR and Australia-origin HMS hovered at US$340-345/t CFR
Chennai. Despite firmer offers, procurement stayed measured as an unfavourable exchange rate and
competitive domestic scrap kept Nhava Sheva HMS bids low at US$310–315/t CFR. Consequently, mills are
actively adjusting their metallic mix toward DRI and pellets to avoid holding high-cost imported
inventories amid sluggish finished-steel sales.
Pakistan: Procurement momentum in Pakistan remained slow as comfortable mill inventories, persistent
monsoon rains, and tepid finished steel consumption reduced buying urgency. Exporters maintained
EU/UK shredded offers at US$415–420/t CFR Port Qasim, facing pushback from domestic mills holding bids
firmly around US$410–412/t CFR. This persistent bid-offer spread restricted fresh bookings, leaving
benchmark shredded assessments flat at US$415/t CFR Port Qasim.
Bangladesh: Import activity in Chattogram remained subdued and selective, weighed down by heavy
monsoon disruptions, slow construction progress, and strict shipment criteria across Asian origins. Deep-
sea HMS 80:20 was indicated at US$370-375/t CFR, while shredded scrap spanned US$390–400/t CFR and
premium Singapore PNS held higher at US$410–415/t CFR. With mills actively avoiding large-volume
commitments to mitigate price risk, seaborne purchases remain confined strictly to immediate
operational requirements
Turkiye: Deep-sea import values held stable, with benchmark US-origin HMS 80:20 assessed at US$375/t
CFR Turkiye as mills showed little urgency after covering their August requirements. European sellers
targeted US$370/t CFR or higher, supported by low Rhine water levels, Black Sea disruptions, and US freight
rates of US$35–36/t. However, persistent weakness in downstream rebar demand continues to prevent
Turkish steelmakers from accepting higher scrap levels for late-September bookings.

Commodities Focus
Chinese coking coal futures in Dalian jumped 15% this week to reach 1,583.50 yuan (US$235) per ton, their
highest valuation since October 2024, as an estimated 50 to 60 million tons of annual capacity in Shanxi
remains offline following extensive safety audits triggered by a major mining incident that initially
shuttered more than 130 million tons of capacity.
In the base metals market, an acute physical squeeze pushed global copper near record peaks as traders
aggressively redirected metal into the United States ahead of potential import tariffs, driving prompt cash
contracts as much as US$545/MT over three-month futures—the widest backwardation since 2021—and
depleting London Metal Exchange inventories by nearly half since mid-May before stabilizing at 207,800
tons with three-month prices settling at US$14,157.50/MT after an earlier 1.7% advance, alongside slight
upticks in aluminum of 0.4% and zinc of 0.3%.
Iron ore futures also slipped toward CNY 700 per ton to hover around 14-month lows, weighed down by
record contractions in Chinese new yuan lending that signal ongoing stagnation across property and
infrastructure development, even as blast furnace operating rates across domestic mills ticked up slightly
by 0.32% points to 82.64%.

WEEK 30 · JULY 24TH, 2026
MARKET OVERVIEW
This week, US tariffs once again took centre stage as the US will collect duties of between 10% and 12.5% on
imports from most major trading partners, its biggest move yet to reconstruct President Donald Trump’s
tariff wall that was struck down by the Supreme Court. President Trump’s tariffs, imposed under Section 301
of the Trade Act of 1974, are facing legal challenges. The duties cover goods from more than 80 countries,
representing 99.4% of U.S. trade, and are officially aimed at combating forced labour. Critics argue the
administration is using Section 301 to recreate the broad tariff regime previously struck down by the
Supreme Court under IEEPA. Legal experts remain divided: some believe the measures exceed the statute’s
intended scope, while others note Section 301 gives the government wide discretion. Businesses are
advised to plan around the tariffs, as court challenges could take considerable time.
On the other hand, the global energy scene is facing unprecedented vulnerability as the secondary
maritime workaround designed to bypass Persian Gulf blockades comes under severe threat. For months,
major Middle Eastern oil producers relied heavily on overland pipeline infrastructure to transfer crude to
western Red Sea terminals, effectively maintaining export volumes despite the near -total closure of the
Strait of Hormuz.
However, this critical alternative route has been severely compromised following an aggressive surge in
maritime strikes along the southern Red Sea corridor. The resumption of regional missile and drone
attacks targeting commercial vessels near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has effectively opened a secondary
maritime front, pushing global crude benchmarks back above one hundred dollars a barrel for the first
time in two months and exposing the extreme fragility of regional bypass strategies.
This sudden escalation along the western coast stems from a rapid deterioration in local political
agreements, culminating in a formal maritime blockade declaration against regional shipping. Following

doubling war-risk insurance premiums overnight and leaving commercial fleet operators with minimal
safe transit options.

DRY BULK | BDI: 2,743 ▼-3.42% (w-o-w)
The global dry bulk market demonstrated underlying resilience, with the benchmark BDI  snapping out of a
multi-day decline at the end of week to rise to 2,743 points. On a weekly comparison, this reflects a
broader cooling of 3.42% across the main index, largely influenced by a turbulent week in the Capesize
segment. Although Capesize spot rates experienced sharp volatility earlier in the week, the BCI rebounded
to 4,285 points as Australian iron ore exports stabilised following a brief eight-hour protected stoppage by
BHP workers at Port Hedland—where average vessel waiting times hit multi-month highs of 8.7 days. In
contrast, BPI dropped to 2,024 points, while the BSI slipped to 1,694 points.
Beyond immediate rate movements, market attention is closely watching key logistical bottlenecks,
particularly in the Panama Canal.

Beyond immediate rate movements, market attention is closely watching key logistical bottlenecks,
particularly in the Panama Canal. Despite reporting strong fiscal third-quarter performance with daily
transits averaging 35 vessels and total transit revenue reaching US$4.8 billion (up 17% y-o-y), the Panama
Canal Authority warned that the probability of a severe El Niño event has surged to 81%. This looming
weather threat raises the strong likelihood of future draft and daily booking restrictions, positioning canal
transit constraints as a critical variable for dry bulk trade flows moving into the second half of the year.
Segment Highlights
Capesize: Capesize faced downward pressure this week as returning vessels delayed by Chinese port
disruptions expanded Pacific tonnage length, driving competition on the West Australia to China route.
Slowing fixture activity across Atlantic long-haul routes and rising bunker costs further dampened
sentiment, though stable iron ore supply from Brazil helped keep the market active. Despite the underlying
spot caution, route averages rebounded from earlier lows, lifting Pacific R/V to US$30,875’s, and T/A trips to
US$46,050’s.
Panamax / Kamsarmax: Panamax drifted softer overall this week as slowing N. Atlantic cargo volumes,
sluggish USG grain activity, and an accumulation of prompt ballast tonnage in the East combined to
weigh down owner sentiment across both basins. While Brazilian grain demand and steady South
American cargo flows initially provided a relative floor, an influx of ballasting ships arriving from Asia
created a two-tier market in the South and capped forward rate momentum. Spot returns faced a general
decline across major routes, dragging T/A rates down to US$20,400’s with Pacific R/V to US$15,550’s.
Supramax / Ultramax: Atlantic rates held a firm yet mixed stance supported by a steady influx of USG and
East Med cargoes against limited prompt tonnage, even as T/A rates slipped to US$28,950’s and F/H trips

Handysize: Handysize remained balanced across Europe this week, while the USG and South Atlantic

this cautious backdrop, spot returns drifted slightly lower, bringing T/A rates down to US$16,750’s and Inter-

CONTAINERS
The global container shipping market continued its post-peak correction this week as the SCFI index fell to
close at 3,062.95 points, driven primarily by easing supply conditions and slowing cargo bookings across
the U.S. West Coast and South America. In contrast, U.S. East Coast routes posted slight rate gains due to
restricted vessel supply tied to extended sailing distances via the Cape of Good Hope, Panama Canal
constraints, and lingering European port backlogs.
Meanwhile, Middle East trades bucked the broader downward trend, surging as escalating security risks in
the Strait of Hormuz—including recent vessel attacks and an Iranian port blockade—prompted a sharp
drop in transits; in response, carriers like Maersk introduced a new US$1,000 per container fee on July 23rd
for Gulf-bound cargo while managing alternative land bridge connections from the Red Sea. Overall, with
lines balancing rate discounts against tactical capacity management and Hapag- Lloyd signalling mid-
July rate defence measures, the market appears positioned for a cycle of moderate corrections and
short-term rebounds rather than a severe drop.

Gaddani, Pakistan: Gadani recyclers are actively seeking candidates amidst an ongoing shortage of
scrap metal. This supply deficit, exacerbated by reduced scrap flows from neighbouring Iran, continues to
provide underlying support for local recycling demand despite a persistent scarcity of available
international tonnage.
Local ship recyclers kept their price offers firm across the board, matching a late-week rally in domestic
steel plate valuations. While end-user consumption has yet to fully match this price surge, market
optimism rests heavily on recent fiscal reforms, including reduced property withholding taxes and
subsidised housing initiatives, which are expected to boost construction activity once the monsoon clears.
Currently, Gadani recyclers remain well-positioned to compete with Indian yards on price.

Aliaga, Turkey: Aliaga recorded a slight positive correction, with both imported raw scrap and domestic
finished steel prices edging up by roughly US$5/MT. However, this slight firming in steel values failed to
boost vessel offers, as cautious yard operators kept purchasing rates unchanged between US$263 ~285
per LDT, leaving Turkish recyclers structurally uncompetitive against South Asian buyers.
This sluggish activity reflects broader domestic financial hurdles, where a continuously weakening Turkish
lira degrades purchasing power for dollar-denominated hulls, and a high central bank interest rate of 37%
makes operational financing exceptionally costly amidst a tight global candidate pool.

India: Imported ferrous scrap trading remained subdued as monsoon disruptions, a weaker Rupee, and
slow rebar sales kept buyers on the sidelines. UK-origin shredded scrap offers were heard above US$390/t
CFR and HMS 80:20 near US$335/t CFR, though no fresh deals were confirmed. Sluggish downstream steel
demand and poor import viability continue to restrict local procurement strictly to immediate operational
needs.
Pakistan: Imported shredded scrap prices strengthened to US$410–US$415/t CFR Port Qasim, supported
by tighter summer supply, higher freight rates, and ongoing transit uncertainty near the Strait of Hormuz.
Notable transactions included a 4,000–4,500 t UK-origin shredded cargo booked at US$408–US$410/t CFR,
alongside Malaysian busheling offers at US$430–US$435/t CFR. However, conservative buyer bids at
US$390–US$395/t CFR maintained a wide bid-offer gap and capped larger volumes.

01Tankers

Suezmax
Petrobras continue to face the brunt of the volatility that this market has to offer. They
fixed 50 points down and 40 points up, all within a span of 2 weeks. Owners who are
able to transit the Gulf of Aden, albeit with conditions have done well with being able
to achieve WS 297.5 for Red Sea to Korea voyage. With the Strait of Hormuz and the
Bab El Mandeb being tricky to transit, suppliers are now looking to off load the oil via
the Sumed pipeline and load out of Sidi Kerir. Charterers in the USG seem to be taking
some cover by taking ships on subs but not much has come to fruition as most of
them have failed.
* CPC has been tested, with W430 on subs with only 3 offers being received, as
owners are clearly pricing in the risk following the recent drone attacks.
Aframax
Rates
* On the other hand, we have a market quote for Med/Skorea that received 8 offers.
Therefore, despite this elevated rate from the Black Sea, it seems unlikely to translate
across the wider market or offset the bearish supply fundamentals, as the majority of
owners will continue to avoid the Black Sea.
* We have plenty of vessels available in the prompt window for WAF, with tonnage
either opening locally or sitting FOC from UKCM positions. In addition, towards the
back end of the fixing window, we have a fleet of ballasters from the East heading
towards the Cape.
* In terms of volume, there will be cargoes to move in the 2nd decade, but a
downward test is anticipated before any congestion emerges.
* Even then, owners are expected to remain pragmatic given the aforementioned
supply outlook. Owners will be banking on the re-emergence of CPC activity and
improved safety assurances to counterbalance the bearish market sentiment.
North Sea
Market activity has been limited as we push into August stems with cargoes covering
quietly with relets and some Suezmax in the mix. The front end of the list has some
natural North Sea tonnage on it for the first time in a couple of weeks.

The Panamax market softened over the course of the week, with the index easing and
sentiment turning more cautious across both basins amid the seasonal summer lull.
The Atlantic set the softer tone – transatlantic and fronthaul enquiry stayed thin,
prompt tonnage was discounted to secure employment, and a widening gap between
owners' ideas and charterers' bids kept activity subdued, even as the Continent and
Western Mediterranean remained comparatively tight on prompt vessels. The Pacific
was the more constructive corner late in the week, steadying off recent lows as North
Pacific grain enquiry improved and charterers returned to cover weather-disrupted
positions, though an ample tonnage list and still-elevated Chinese stockpiles capped
the recovery. Period interest remained active, with charterers continuing to pursue
Kamsarmax cover for one- to two-year employment, but bid and offer stayed apart
and owners of modern eco tonnage were reluctant to chase the market lower. On
balance we would characterise the tone as soft but stabilising into month-end, with
near-term direction hinging on whether the Pacific's tentative firming can broaden
and Atlantic cargo replenishment comes through.
Supramax/Ultramax market remained under pressure, extending its recent downward
trend as fresh cargo enquiry stayed limited across most regions. Atlantic sentiment
continued to soften, with increasing vessel availability weighing on in despite
Rates
occasional stronger fixtures. Asia remains relatively quiet. Overall, the market remains
cautious with little sign of a near-term improvement in the coming weeks. The Handy
market was largely unchanged, with sentiment continuing to be driven by vessel
positioning rather than any meaningful shift in demand. The Continent/Mediterranean
remained balanced but subdued, while the Atlantic softened further as an expanding
tonnage list outpaced fresh cargo volumes. Activity in the Pacific was generally quiet,
with limited fixing keeping momentum subdued.

Week 31 | Tuesday 04th August 2026
Market Insight
By George Vitsos, Offshore Broker
The Offshore sector has been greatly affected by the current geo-
political situation, as challenges that are substantially greater
than those faced by merchant vessels are presented, due to the
limited flexibility the floating units have under tow. Floating rigs,
accommodation units, crane barges, vessels and FPSOs that are
being repositioned, typically move at speeds of only 4 -7 knots
and are unable to take evasive action, as their slow speed, pre-
dictable movements and large radar signature make them partic-
ularly vulnerable targets in any environment where missiles,
drones, unmanned surface vessels or small craft attacks are pos-
sible. The International Maritime Organization has repeatedly
highlighted that commercial shipping and seafarers are increas-
ingly exposed to geopolitical conflicts, while maritime security
experts continue to warn that vessels operating in both Hormuz
and the Red Sea face elevated risks regardless of nationality or
flag.
The Strait of Hormuz currently represents the most difficult envi-
ronment for offshore movements. In practice, a towing operation
might not only require just the tug and the tow, but also support
crafts, fuel logistics, crew changes, emergency response arrange-
ments and reliable Ports of Refuge. Recent attacks on several
tankers in the Middle East and Red Sea, are still exposed to mili-
tary actions, whereas hundreds of tankers remain anchored or
drifting throughout the Gulf awaiting improved security condi-
tions, creating significant navigational congestion. Reports of very
low daily transit numbers compared with normal trading patterns
indicate a de facto restriction on navigation, even if the waterway
remains open.
For offshore contractors, the immediate consequence is that find-
ing suitable ocean -going tugs able to enter or exit the Gulf has
become increasingly difficult. From a commercial standpoint,
many operators are reluctant to expose crews to a region where
vessels have been struck by projectiles, drones or explosive craft.
From an insurance perspective, war -risk premiums have risen
sharply, and underwriters are scrutinizing every planned voyage.
The recent decision by Lloyd's market participants to terminate
coverage for vessels making unauthorized transit payments or
tolls in the Strait of Hormuz adds a further layer of uncertainty to

From an insurance perspective, war -risk premiums have risen
sharply, and underwriters are scrutinizing every planned voyage.
The recent decision by Lloyd's market participants to terminate
coverage for vessels making unauthorized transit payments or
tolls in the Strait of Hormuz adds a further layer of uncertainty to
voyage.
The Red Sea presents similar concerns. Although some commer-
cial traffic continues to pass through Bab el -Mandeb, Houthi at-
tacks have demonstrated a threat to vessels over a wide geo-
graphic area using drones and missiles, while maritime security
advisories continue to classify the southern Red Sea, Gulf of Aden
and Bab el -Mandeb Strait as high -threat risk areas, with the
Houthis recently escalating their campaign through renewed
threats against shipping and the announcement of restrictions
targeting Saudi -linked maritime trade. Security organizations
have reported evidence of vessel diversions and reduced traffic
levels in the Bab el -Mandeb area, underlining the ongoing opera-
tional challenges for commercial shipping.
For a large tanker, the exposure window in Bab el -Mandeb may
be measured in hours. For a tow moving at four knots, the same
exposure can extend across several days, significantly increasing
operational risk. As a result, offshore operators contemplating the
mobilization of commercial vessels, rigs, barges or floating pro-
duction units into or out of the Gulf should expect restricted tug
availability, elevated insurance costs and potential difficulties ob-
taining charter -party and lender approvals. Industry feedback
from sources active in the region already suggest that many tug
operators are unwilling to undertake Hormuz transits under pre-
sent conditions, effectively limiting available towing capacity.
Developments during the past week have further demonstrated
how quickly the threat environment can evolve. Reports of re-
duced transit levels through both Hormuz and Bab el -Mandeb,
together with renewed attacks and threats directed against com-
mercial shipping and energy infrastructure, continue to influence
operator decision -making and insurance market sentiment. For
offshore projects requiring prolonged exposure within these are-
as, the risk profile remains substantially higher than that faced by
conventional merchant shipping.

Last week, the large crude carrier rates firmed, supported by re-
newed disruptions in Middle East resulting to longer -haul diver-
sions via Suez, while the Aframax market corrected, reversing the
strong performance recorded in previous weeks. The BDTI aver-
aged 2,592, up 7% w- o-w.
The VLCC segment strengthened, underpinned by Middle East
activity despite heightened geopolitical risks. The decline in Irani-
an attacks in the Arabian Gulf encouraged owners to load in the
Gulf of Oman. Red Sea also added ton miles, with some crude
flows moving through Suez and via the SUMED pipeline and
around the Cape of Good Hope. West African rates rose as prompt
tonnage tightened, though stronger demand is needed to sustain
the gains. The US Gulf firmed amid robust enquiry, which ab-
sorbed tonnage and strengthened rates and sentiment.
Geopolitical risk and navigational safety remain a key driver of the
Suezmax market, with the two major trading regions, Black Sea
and Middle East, exposed to ongoing hostilities. Although activity
eased in Black Sea, overall rates firmed as heightened security
risks and recurring disruptions to CPC operations lifted premiums.
At the same time, ballasting vessels to alternative markets in-
creased tonnage availability in West Africa, placing rates and sen-
timent under pressure. Elsewhere, the Atlantic basin found some
support from a pickup in Guyanese crude cargoes.

The dry bulk sector followed contrasting trends last week, as
smaller-vessel rates declined, Capesize earnings remained stable,
and Panamax rates strengthened. Overall, the BDI averaged
2,680, representing a modest 1% week-on-week decrease.
The Capesize spot market remained broadly steady, strengthen-
ing after midweek as demand recovered in the South Atlantic and
Pacific, supported in the latter by increased miner participation.
The North Atlantic was the weakest region, where only sporadic
transatlantic demand emerged, being insufficient to lift sentiment
or generate meaningful upward momentum.
The Kamsarmax/Panamax segment firmed, recovering from earli-
er subdued conditions. Rates strengthened progressively as in-
creased Atlantic demand coincided with a limited pool of available
vessels, improving market sentiment. The Pacific also gained mo-
mentum, with demand concentrated on North Pacific grain car-
goes and Australian coal shipments. Combined with constrained
supply, this stronger cargo flow supported higher spot rates.

due to weak cargo demand across most regions. The US Gulf was

The Ultramax/Supramax market softened last week, primarily
due to weak cargo demand across most regions. The US Gulf was
a relative bright spot, showing signs of recovery as fixing activity
increased. The South Atlantic experienced its seasonal slowdown,
limiting activity and rate gains. Asian and Pacific markets re-
mained under pressure from scarce enquiries and excess ton-
nage. In the Mediterranean, demand was uneven, with favourably
positioned vessels securing better employment opportunities.
On the Handysize side, fundamentals pressured rates, as con-
strained demand left both basins with excess supply and shaped
a market backdrop short of the cargo volume needed to absorb
open tonnage. This was most evident in the US Gulf, South Atlan-
tic and North Pacific. In the Mediterranean and Continent, with
few fresh cargoes emerging, employment prospects and fixing
levels came down to vessel position, making regional trade posi-
tion driven rather than demand led.

Last week, ship recycling markets across the Subcontinent wit-
nessed a more positive sentiment, supported by increased de-
mand for recycling candidates.
India's ship recycling market improved modestly from the sub-
dued conditions of the previous week, underpinned by stronger,
albeit selective, buying interest. Steel fundamentals remained
weak as monsoons continued to constrain output. Neverthe-
less, dollar -denominated plate prices rose as the Indian rupee
strengthened against the US dollar. Although India remained
less price-competitive than its Subcontinent peers, it continued
to reinforce its competitive advantage through regulatory com-
pliance. With the majority of yards being HKC -compliant and the
recent proposal to add two Indian yards to the EU List, the
country is further enhancing its position, potentially paving the
way for EU-flagged candidates.
Chattogram's market outlook has become more positive, sup-
ported by stronger tonnage demand, the approaching end of the
monsoon season, and the return of recycling candidates delayed
by last month ’s severe flooding, creating a healthy tonnage
pool. Purchasing appetite favors bulkers, general cargo vessels,
and units with clean records, while sanctions -related histories
continue to depress prices. Steel market activity has recovered
and plate prices remain firm, but recyclers have not yet reflect-
ed this strength in their offers.

Week 28 | Tuesday 14th July 2026
Market Insight
By Nikos Tagoulis, Senior Analyst
The MoU between Washington and Tehran in mid -June, which set
out a 60 -day framework for reaching a final settlement, briefly
raised hopes that the Hormuz crisis was moving toward a stable
resolution. Those expectations soon faded. Over the past week,
renewed Iranian attacks on commercial vessels transiting the
strait, prompted Washington to reinstate the oil export sanctions
suspended under the agreement. The ceasefire effectively col-
lapsed as the US and Iran exchanged airstrikes, commercial ship-
ping came under renewed attack, Tehran again declared Hormuz
closed and vessel traffic fell sharply, reversing the recovery in
transits recorded in late June and early July. Beyond the immedi-
ate hostilities, the broader question of how passage through the
waterway will ultimately be governed remains unresolved, leav-
ing the region caught between further escalation and another
attempt at de-escalation.
For shipping markets, the deeper consequence lies in the erosion
of confidence in any settlement. This is the third arrangement to
break down since February, and each new understanding is in-
creasingly viewed as provisional. Against this backdrop, charter-
ers are adopting a more cautious stance, monitoring how the sit-
uation unfolds, while prolonged instability is likely to make more
owners reluctant to deploy tonnage to the Middle East Gulf.
The spot market's reaction to the July flare -up illustrates how
sensitive freight pricing has become to geopolitical signals. TD3C
earnings, which had corrected to below $290,000 per day once
the post -memorandum rally unwound, turned sharply higher as
hostilities resumed, climbing by 18% within four trading days to
around $344,000. Swings of this magnitude within a single week
have become a recurring feature of the market since the crisis
began, with rates responding primarily to headlines rather than
underlying cargo flows.
The longer the disruption persists, the more firmly alternative
suppliers and routes entrench their position within the market.
The United States has ramped up its oil and LNG exports, rein-
forcing its role as a key energy supplier, while other Atlantic basin
producers, including Brazil, Canada and West Africa, are also ex-
