This week on Capesize we saw strong demand from Pacific C5 as three majors were seen in the market alongside a healthy showing of supportive operators. Recent bids seen at mid to high USD 15 levels and today a Newcastlemax fixed at low USD 15 C5 equivalent. Ballasters are looking to get ahead of yet another Typhoon forecasted to hit the coast of southeast China (near Fujian) around late Thursday to early Friday and recent fixtures ex West Australia have been reported in high USD 14s. Atlantic C3 Brazil/China has also seen healthy activity with rumors expecting even higher levels for October. With a flurry of fixtures yesterday, C3 ex Brazil reported levels for 2h September laycans in mid/high USD 37s with one stem reported at USD 38 for late September. Offers today reported in high USD 37 and mid USD 38s for early October
laycans ex Brazil. The North Atlantic shows some fronthaul and transatlantic demand ex Seven Islands for later September dates and tonnage remains healthy in the North. A recent fixture ex Seven Islands to India was reported in low USD 42 for end September.

text: The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the index posting consecutive gains and sentiment improving across both basins. The Pacific has been the clearer engine: NoPac and Australian grain and coal demand has absorbed the prompt tonnage that had been weighing on the market, and owners are now comfortable holding their levels while charterers chase. In the Atlantic the North has been the steadier of the two, supported by a healthy coal and minerals programme into the Continent that has kept fronthaul well bid, while the South Atlantic has traded more sideways as the market looks toward the next grain window and owners show little urgency to discount. Period enquiry has picked up noticeably, with a wider range of owners and operators willing to engage on one-year business, although bids continue to sit modestly behind owners' ideas. With paper firmer and tonnage tightening into September, we expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer in the near term.

text: The Supramax market remained largely subdued and stable. The Atlantic was mixed, with the Mediterranean gradually softening while the Continent saw some fresh enquiry and the US Gulf and South Atlantic remained broadly balanced. In the Pacific, activity was stronger in the NOPAC and parts of Southeast Asia, while Indonesian coal activity was relatively limited. The Handysize market showed a modestly firmer tone, supported by improving cargos in East Coast South America, tighter prompt tonnage in parts of the Pacific and better sentiment in the US Gulf. While the US Gulf was still soft in the short term despite expectations of improvement ahead.

text:
We are currently going through the third distinct phase of Middle East exports since the Hormuz crisis began. After suffering an immediate loss of around 15 mb/d of export capacity in the spring months and then experiencing the short-lived reopening during the second half of July, we are now in a phase of increased tanker shuttling, which has become very prominent since early August with volumes estimated to have reached ~4.5 mb/d. Middle Eastern producers, along with a handful of risk-tolerant tanker operators, have moved cargoes through the Strait of Hormuz to Ship-To-Ship hubs off Oman and Fujairah, where the volumes are transferred onto other tankers for onward delivery. The strategy has been more effective at getting stranded cargoes back into the market, even as attacks on vessels transiting Hormuz continue, as exporters are now assuming a greater share of the transit risk. All signs indicate a higher risk tolerance from producers, with UAE’s biggest crude exporters seeking pathways of bringing cargoes to market, relying on Ship-To-Ship shuttles to move trapped cargo.
Notably, average VLCC spot rates have climbed to their highest levels since the start of the US-Iran conflict, with modern vessels earning TCEs of USD 800,000 per day on voyages through the SoH. In terms of enquiries, we are observing increased interest in the larger tanker segments spanning Aframax upto VLCC, with units that can give prompt delivery being at the forefront of attention. At the same time vintage tonnage is experiencing a notable revival in demand.
The Bulker sector continues to advance through the second half of the year on a solid footing, with fleet growth of 3.5–4% on track to be achieved this year, although the repercussions of the Black Sea and Middle East remain uncertain. This week ended on a positive note for the dry spot market, with the Capesize BDI closing at 5,536, up ~17% from last week’s close while we monitored notable activity in the Supramax and Ultramax segments, with enquiries primarily focused on units around 15 years of age.

In the USG, demand for Supramax/Ultramax tonnage is gradually picking up this week. While owners are attempting to push rates higher when negotiating fronthaul routes, this is off the table for transatlantic and short inter-Caribs trips. Competition for these cargoes remains quite fierce among owners, as most prefer to keep their carriers within the Atlantic while waiting for the US grain export season to kick off. Meanwhile, the USG Handy segment remains under pressure, though cargo flow is starting to recover. At the moment, shipment of 25-30,000 t of corn or soybeans from New Orleans to EgyptMed costs high $30s/t bss 1/1.
The ECSA Supramax/Ultramax market has seen a slowdown in activity following last week’s surge. Nevertheless, rates are holding at levels comfortable for owners, and the market has entered a wait-and-see mode ahead of the next wave of cargo traffic upturn. At the same time, Handy rates stay depressed in the South Atlantic. Thus, rates for transportation of 25- 30,000 t of wheat from Upriver to Algeria still amount to high $40s/t in case of 5000 sshex dischrate or low $50s/t in case of 2500 sshex dischrate. Prospects for a future recovery directly depend on dynamics in neighboring regions, primarily the USG. “It remains to be seen if USG will attract vessels open in ECSA or not,” a local broker commented to ISM.
As expected, the number of new cargo offers from Baltic & Continent ports is gradually rising, while the surplus of tonnage is no longer seen in the region. Handysize owners are feeling increasingly confident, with freight levels up by $1-2k daily and $0.5-1/t over

text:
Diplomatic discussions between regional authorities have introduced a new framework for managing the Strait of Hormuz, outlining a roadmap toward a temporary navigational channel and coordinated mine- clearing initiatives. Under this structure, negotiators are evaluating a dual-lane transit corridor where vessels would enter the Persian Gulf through northern designated waters and exit via southern lanes, followed by further discussions to establish permanent operational and security arrangements. However, significant hurdles remain, particularly regarding demands to close the existing southern route along the Omani coastline and potential methods for maritime service administration. With stakeholders continuing to reject any framework that imposes passage conditions or compromises absolute freedom of navigation, fleet operators remain cautious about an immediate, unencumbered return to the waterway.
Despite the persistent threat, crude outflows from the Persian Gulf have quietly rebounded as regional producers utilise shuttle networks to move shut-in volumes onto the global market. Daily volumes passing out of the region have climbed back toward an estimated 6~8 million barrels, supported by major loading surges across key export facilities in Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia. To circumvent security risks, producers are increasingly relying on dedicated shuttle tankers to transport crude just beyond the strait, where cargoes are transferred to awaiting international carriers anchored off coastal bunkering hubs. This revival of seaborne flows has exerted downward pressure on international crude benchmarks, driving futures back toward US$88 a barrel and delivering the sharpest weekly price softening in two months.
This model has created unprecedented profitability for tanker operators willing to navigate the high-risk zone, with freight earnings for VLCCs touching historic highs. Energy majors and trading houses are capitalising on significant price discounts on inland barrels, absorbing elevated shipping costs that equate to roughly US$10 per barrel to deliver cargoes to worldwide refining hubs. However, the market remains sharply bifurcated; while crude supply chains are gradually adapting and softening prompt oil benchmarks, refined product markets continue to face severe tightness.
With substantial regional refining capacity still offline and international processing assets facing overseas disruptions, downstream fuel segments like diesel and gasoline are seeing sustained upward margin pressure, highlighting an uneven recovery across the global maritime trade.

**Capesize:** Capesize rebounded this week, driven by a surge in Western Australian iron ore shipments alongside prompt tonnage tightening as ballasters maneuvered around another incoming typhoon off southeast China. Active participation from major miners pushed Pacific C5 rates higher, while steady Guinean bauxite and iron ore stems helped absorb long-haul capacity to keep the Atlantic market well supported. Reflecting these firm market conditions, spot returns posted solid gains across key benchmarks, lifting Transatlantic rates to US$48,450’s and Pacific r/v to US$44,750’s per day.
**Panamax / Kamsarmax:** Panamax experienced a mixed week as the 5TC average fell under the weight of regional tonnage overcapacity and ballast vessel inflows, even as grain demand showed signs of recovery. Route rates diverged, with Inni R/V climbing to US$16,070’s while F/H dropped sharply to US$27,060’s. Although improving grain volumes and firmer paper provide downside support, spot rates are likely to remain range-bound until surplus Pacific tonnage clears and coal shipments rebound.
**Supramax / Ultramax:** Supramax edged up this week as steady long-haul cargo flows from the South Atlantic, the USG, and NOPAC helped absorb prompt vessel capacity. While the overall market maintained a balanced yet subdued tone, ongoing vessel oversupply across Europe and the Mediterranean alongside reduced Indonesian coal exports capped more broad-based momentum. Reflecting these modest regional gains, spot returns nudged upward on key routes, lifting Pacific r/v to US$16,450’s and Transatlantic to US$27,050’s.
**Handysize:** Handysize displayed a modestly firmer tone this week, supported by improving cargo volumes in EC South America and better forward sentiment in the USG, even as the Mediterranean faced persistent pressure from ample tonnage availability. Across the Pacific, Asian routes held relatively steady, drawing underlying support from pockets of fresh activity and tight prompt vessel supply. Reflecting these modest regional gains, spot returns edged upward across key routes, lifting Inter-Pacific runs to US$16,200’s and fronthaul trips to US$11,600’s per day.

text:
Container shipping market continued its climb this week as the SCFI rose to 3,509.54 points. Spot rates were primarily underpinned by tight vessel capacity and resilient demand across the Americas and South America, where carrier-initiated General Rate Increases and Peak Season Surcharges lifted East Coast rates by 9.6% and West Coast rates by 13.2%. Severe typhoon disruptions and equipment bottlenecks at Chinese departure hubs further restricted short-sea turnaround times, causing Southeast Asian freight rates to jump sharply.
Meanwhile, severe operational constraints across the Persian Gulf continue to keep Middle East rate baselines firm, as functional limitations at Jebel Ali have diverted cargo flows into neighbouring hubs such as Fujairah, Khor Fakkan, and Oman. This prolonged friction is actively reshaping global trade patterns, as reflected in Alphaliner’s first-half port rankings: Dubai plummeted from 10th to 32nd place after handling
3.14 million TEU compared to 7.77 million TEU the previous year, and Abu Dhabi’s Khalifa Port saw volumes tumble by over 50%. In contrast, Malaysia’s Port Klang stepped into 10th position with an estimated 7.7 million TEU, while Los Angeles and Long Beach held 9th place with a combined 9.97 million TEU. Leading the list, Shanghai retained the top position by handling 28.74 million TEU (up 6.2%), while Ningbo- Zhoushan grew 8.8% to 22.90 million TEU, aided by its Jintang Phase II expansion, which expanded volumes by 23.4% and added 17 international routes, narrowly overtaking Singapore (22.74 million TEU, up 4.7%) for second place.

**Alang, India:** Alang maintained a steady week, with keen buying interest driving a noticeable improvement in sentiment. Supported by an active recovery in local scrap demand, domestic plate prices settled at 41,000 rupees/MT by Friday. This provides yard operators with a welcome margin cushion compared to the US$423 mark seen at the start of the period. While Indian buyers still have some ground to cover before matching the higher pricing levels offered for conventional bulkers and containers in Bangladesh and Pakistan, the sustained uptick in local steel values and healthy plot fundamentals offer genuine encouragement as the market heads toward the fourth quarter.
This is reinforced by solid macroeconomic fundamentals across the broader Indian economy. The Reserve Bank of India continues to maintain an accommodative policy stance with the benchmark repo rate steady at 5.25%, backed by a robust full-year economic growth projection of 6.7% and an expanding foreign exchange reserve cushion near US$707 billion.
Domestic steel consumption is projected to expand by over 9% this year, powered by heavy government capital outlays in transportation infrastructure, railway modernisation, and urban housing schemes. As seasonal monsoon rains taper off and construction activity accelerates across the country, this expanding industrial appetite for rerollable scrap provides Alang’s recyclers with a reliable domestic floor to pursue fresh tonnage with increasing confidence.

**Copper** futures advanced above US$6.7 per pound to establish a fresh historical peak, driven by persistent global supply constraints and sustained cargo diversions toward the United States ahead of potential tariff decisions. This upward momentum is further reinforced by London Metal Exchange inventories shrinking by nearly half since mid-May, acute concentrate shortages among Chinese smelters, and flooding at the Kamoa-Kakula operation in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which threatens to trim Zijin Mining's production share by as much as 57,000 tons this year.
In the ferrous complex, raw material prices are beginning to decouple from finished steel; **iron ore** futures moved higher toward CNY 720 per ton, recovering from 14-month lows as mills increased blast furnace utilisation in anticipation of seasonal pre-winter restocking and supportive policy guidance from Beijing.
**Steel** rebar futures dropped to a four-week low of approximately CNY 3,070 per ton under the weight of high inventory levels, lower year-on-year home prices in July, and compressed margins that left only about one-third of domestic steelmakers profitable at month-end, though directives from the National Development and Reform Commission to accelerate major construction projects continue to provide an underlying floor for long-term consumption.

**shows**
The number of vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz was little changed on Monday compared with the weekend, hovering around five, preliminary ship-tracking data showed, below the 10-day average of around 14. Four of the vessels entered the strait and one exited, data from Kpler showed.
##### Port Hedland unions place wage deal counterproposal to BHP ahead
##### of September 8 talks
The Combined BHP Ports Unions has placed a counterproposal on a wage deal for workers at its Port Hedland operations in Western Australia ahead of their next meeting on September 8, it said on Tuesday, after workers rejected a proposal from BHP. "We continue to make progress towards an agreement that will address key areas raised by our workforce," a BHP spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
##### Mizuho Bank files case against Radiant World in Singapore
Japan's Mizuho Bank Ltd has filed a case against the Singapore operating entity of iron ore trader Radiant World in the city-state's Supreme Court, according to the court's website. Mizuho Bank, the banking unit of Mizuho Financial Group, is seeking an injunction against Radiant World Corporation, a court listing showed on Friday. The court listing did not provide details of the injunction sought.
##### Chile's copper output declines 9.4% in July hit by severe weather
Copper output in Chile, the world's largest producer of the metal, fell
9.4% year-on-year in July hit by severe storms that struck mining operation areas, statistics agency INE said on Monday. Chile saw its
copper output down at 403,424 metric tons from 445,322 tons on the same month a year earlier.

##### drag on output
Chilean state miner Codelco on Friday reported sharply stronger first-half earnings as higher copper prices outweighed weaker production and higher costs, while new Chief Executive Jorge Gomez said the company's priority was to restore productivity after setbacks at key mines. Codelco reported pre-tax profit of $1.97 billion for the first half of 2026, up more than fourfold from the $429 million posted in the same period a year earlier.

**exports**
Up to 70 vessels are waiting near the Danube's Sulina Canal for access to Ukrainian ports to load grain for export, traders and analysts said on Wednesday, with a shortage of pilots and priority given to other cargoes creating long delays. After Russian attacks effectively blocked Ukraine's Black Sea ports, which had handled 90% of the country's grain exports, some shipments were rerouted through Danube river ports, which have much lower capacity.
##### Russian grain exports shift to Baltic as Black Sea trade disrupted
Russian grain exporters are rerouting shipments to the Baltic Sea, including ports in the Baltic states, after Ukrainian drone attacks in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov forced them to seek alternative routes, traders and analysts told Reuters on Monday. Russia and Ukraine have been pounding each other's export terminals and grain-carrying vessels in the Black Sea, creating the biggest
disruption to Black Sea trade since the conflict in Ukraine began more than four years ago.
##### Heat, floods threaten China crops as U.S. farm purchases loom
High temperatures and heavy rain have battered China's key corn, soybean and cotton-growing regions since mid-July, threatening crop quality and yield losses that could boost imports of feed grains and cotton, including from the United States. China pledged to buy $17 billion of U.S. agricultural goods annually through 2028, excluding soybeans, under a trade war truce, the White House has said.
##### Australia to produce more wheat after better than expected rain
The outlook for Australia's wheat harvest has improved thanks to timely rainfall in many cropping areas, which should give the world's No. 3 wheat exporter more to ship into a global market that has tightened in recent months, driving up prices. Four analysts said they now expect Australia to produce around 30 million to 32 million metric tons of wheat this year.

##### Asia's crude oil imports stay soft in August, challenging US Hormuz claims
Asia's imports of crude oil in August are still well short of levels prior to the start of the Iran conflict, raising further questions as to just how much crude is actually leaving the Middle East. The top-importing continent is expected to see arrivals of 23.12 million barrels per day in August, slightly down from July's
23.36 million bpd, according to data compiled by commodity analysts Kpler.
##### Trump says US will refill Strategic Petroleum Reserve using Venezuelan oil
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that oil from a recently struck deal with Venezuela will be used to replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has been drawn down sharply in recent years to respond to global supply disruptions and high fuel prices. Trump said in a social media post that the "topping out" process will begin shortly, describing the Venezuelan oil as a “Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.”
##### Trump's oil deal with Venezuela raises red flags for some major
**producers**
An unprecedented deal for the U.S. to gain access to a fifth of Venezuela's oil reserves-and the central role a Venezuelan businessman will play-is prompting questions and hesitation from some oil companies evaluating potential investments in the country, sources familiar with the situation told Reuters. A White House fact sheet released late on Monday outlined an arrangement under which private oil firm North American Blue Energy Partners would receive a 100-year
lease for 17 oilfields in Venezuela holding some 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. The U.S. will take a 35% equity stake in the corporate parent company, receive a guaranteed 20% of the oil production and hold a right-of-first-refusal to purchase all of the remaining output.

Iran's energy hub of Kharg Island is being blown to smithereens, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday in a one-line social media post accompanied by an AI- generated video clip. There was no other evidence that the Iranian energy hub was under attack. The White House and the U.S. Defense Department did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours.

##### Depleted US oil stash loses potency as Iran war grinds on
Six months into the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, Washington may find it harder to calm jittery oil markets after U.S. presidents drained the aging Strategic Petroleum Reserve over the last five years. The SPR, which Washington created after the oil crises of the 1970s, holds crude in a series of 60 underground salt caverns along the coasts of Texas and Louisiana. After years of releases by former President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump, the reserve is at its lowest level since 1982, holding just 289.7 million barrels.

**drilling**
The U.S. Interior Department is preparing to ease environmental review requirements for some oil and gas exploration activities in

The deterioration became significantly more visible in August. As of August 26, combined recorded loadings stand at only 2.13 million MT, comprising 1.76 million MT from Russia and just 0.37 million MT from Ukraine. These figures re- main incomplete and should improve as month-end operations are recorded, yet the current gap is too large to be ex- plained purely by timing. Since July, attacks on port facilities, terminals and commercial vessels have intensified across the region. Ukrainian deepwater ports have operated under severe pressure, while Russian grain terminals around Novorossiysk and navigation through parts of the Azov-Black Sea system have also faced disruption. Market reports indicate that these attacks have delayed cargoes, restricted export capacity and made owners increasingly reluctant to commit tonnage without substantially higher freight and war-risk compensation.

text:
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is becoming more precarious by the hour as the US-Iran conflict has intensified again. Several tankers have been hit, and reports suggest that a fully laden VLCC has been abandoned by its crew. The possibility of a major oil spill would of course be a natural disaster but will also bring more focus on the condition of ships which do make it through and their safety when it comes to performing ship to ship operations. A number of discounted Somo tenders never made it through the strait resulting in some failures of fixtures done in the last couple of days at inflated rates. With that some of the immediate pressure has eased slightly, but the position list still remains wanting and rates are unlikely to go much down any time soon. The Atlantic position list is even more challenging, and the likes of oil major Petrobras reportedly only had 1 offer yesterday for a Brazil/China enquiry by the deadline, on and ex d/d ship which wasn’t workable. There’s also reports of another Brazilian export cargo working off the market. Add to that a couple of charterers
sniffing ex West Africa and a tender or two USG/Eastbound and it’s a perfect “storm”. Arguably the Suezmax market has seen a drop lately and will eventually cap the upside for their bigger sisters.

North Sea After a long weekend activity has been slow on the pick up. Natural dates 8-10 window but with a number of relets around and stems a little thin charterers are able to take their time. US market looks to have bottomed and with Mediterranean market looking softer we may see drive to ballast towards the US again after a quiet few days on that front. Slow but steady.
Mediterranean Activity stalled at the end of last week which has rebuilt the early part of the list. Activity has picked up again at the start of the week but the increased tonnage has changed the sentiment for now and charterers have managed to pushed the market down. Natural window pushing into the 2nd decade with tonnage to clear which in the short term may lead to some more weakening before we find the bottom.

text:
Capesize is heating up across all segments, with both C3 and C5 trade routes posting some of the highest numbers seen this year. Last done on C3 Brazil/China today was seen at USD 40.9, setting a new benchmark which hasn't been seen since the peak of
2021. FFAs are up for the coming quarter, Baltic C3 prints USD 40.2 today and C5 is also showing strong activity with last done in the mid USD 16s and rumors of a fixture at USD 17 flat (yet to be confirmed). C5 West Australia/China prints USD 16.5 today on the Baltic, jumping 7.59% today, overtaking C3 Brazil/China as the higher earner per day between C3 and C5. With an uptick of ballasters headed for Brazil toward the end
of September, we may see some pressure in the Atlantic for late September and early October laycans. Overall sentiment is bullish but cautious as limited fresh demand to absorb growing supply.

text: The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the gains broadening across both basins as the index pushed higher over successive sessions. In the Atlantic the tone is constructive: transatlantic business remains well bid on the back of a replenished cargo book and a tightening nearby tonnage list, while fronthaul has been slower to follow, with owners holding above charterers' ideas on US Gulf and South American grain. The Pacific has been the stronger of the two, where a steady flow of Australian and Indonesian coal alongside North Pacific grain has left prompt tonnage short and charterers chasing owners' levels rather than the reverse. Period interest has picked up markedly, with a good spread of owners collecting for both short and twelve-month cover and bids increasingly obliged to follow last-done rather than set it, although the forward curve continues to price modest backwardation beyond the prompt. We expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer into next week, with the main question being how much of the recent move reflects genuine incremental demand rather than positioning ahead of the autumn grain programme.

text: The Supramax market remained mixed and largely directionless, with activity picking up selectively across both the Atlantic and Asia. The Atlantic saw pockets of strength, particularly around the USG and South Atlantic, supported by steady demand for grains, petcoke and minor bulks, while Asia remained active but positional with varied tonnage availability between areas. Handysize trading was generally subdued, although fundamentals remained healthy in parts of the Pacific and South Atlantic. The US Gulf continued to show relatively firm conditions despite limited fixing, while the Continent and Mediterranean markets remained softer. Overall, sentiment across both sectors remains cautious, with regional tonnage positioning and pockets of enquiry driving the market rather than any clear broader trend. There is good appetite for period with quite a few fixtures reported past weeks.

S&P activity has remained on an overall strong course as we have entered September month. Freight rates maintain very high numbers across both dry and wet spaces, which continue to underpin asset prices and S&P appetite, albeit the uncertainty associated with the ongoing geopolitical disturbances in the Black Sea and the Middle East.
More specifically, this Friday, Capesize spot rates reached $58,000 per day, representing new multi-year highs, namely since December 2023 when they briefly reached $60,000. To capitalize on the firm earnings particularly driven by the Atlantic basin, Cape / Nuke buyers are coming on the market, with the sweet spot appearing to be units at ~10-20 years of age. For reference a 15-year-old Japan built Cape is priced in the region of high USD 30’s m today representing roughly a 70% increase in value over a same aged ship in December 2023. Moreover, a healthy number of enquiries for both Eco and Non- Eco ~10-15-year-old Panamaxes and Kamsarmaxes has been observed with a slight preference toward Japan builds.
Tankers are closing the week stronger after some volatility in rates, with eco VLCC and MR earnings rebounding 15.5% and 17.6%, respectively, from last week’s close. At the same time, the Strait of Hormuz has become more uneasy with several tankers reportedly attacked, while market players engaging with trades in the region enjoying lucrative returns. Aframax to VLCC tonnage that can give prompt delivery remains scarce and highly sought after, although we now also observe rekindled buying appetite for product tankers, ranging from MR1 to LR1.

Market Insight
By Nikos Tagoulis, Senior Analyst
The EUA market maintained its upward trend in August, despite
the quieter trading conditions and lower liquidity that typically
characterize the holiday period. The advance extended the recov-
ery that began in late March and left the EU ETS on a constructive
footing heading into autumn. The Front Dec -26 EUA contract av-
eraged €82.36 /ton during August and at the time of writing read
€83.30 /ton, around 6.5% above the 2026 y -t-d average. Prices
remained within a relatively narrow range during the month, and
the contract continued to trade above its 50 -, 100- and 200-day
moving averages.
The European gas market has contributed to the firming of EUAs.
Prices at the Dutch TTF hub rose significantly as geopolitical ten-
sions leading to Qatari volumes off market, low European storage
levels and competition from Asian buyers for LNG cargoes height-
ened concerns over winter supply.
Although the correlation between front-month TTF gas prices and
EUAs fluctuated in August, it has strengthened recently, suggest-
ing that prevailing gas -market dynamics are supporting EUA de-
mand. The principal transmission channel is fuel -switching eco-
nomics: higher gas prices make coal more competitive with gas
for power generation, encouraging more carbon -intensive output
and increasing utilities’ demand for allowances.
Furthermore, recent economic signals add to this supportive
backdrop, pointing to firm industrial demand. The August euro-
zone manufacturing PMI reached its strongest level in more than
four years, accompanied by stronger new orders, a recovery in
exports and the first increase in factory employment after more
than three years. Together, these developments strengthen the
outlook for EUA demand.
Despite the positive backdrop, traders remain cautious. Invest-
ment funds have reduced their net -long exposure in recent
weeks, while commercial participants have continued to increase
their forward exposure, reflecting hedging strategies built around
expectations of further EUA price increases. The divergence indi-
cates that commercial buying remains driven by risk management
even as speculative interest weakens. Compliance buying adds
another source of demand ahead of September 30, including from

Despite the positive backdrop, traders remain cautious. Invest-
ment funds have reduced their net -long exposure in recent
weeks, while commercial participants have continued to increase
their forward exposure, reflecting hedging strategies built around
expectations of further EUA price increases. The divergence indi-
cates that commercial buying remains driven by risk management
even as speculative interest weakens. Compliance buying adds
another source of demand ahead of September 30, including from
shipping companies as the maritime sector ’s obligations continue
to phase in. In 2026, shipping companies must surrender allow-
ances covering 70% of their verified 2025 emissions within the
scope of the EU ETS, rising to 100% of 2026 emissions in the fol-
lowing year, with higher EUA prices increasing the compliance
cost of voyages covered by the scheme.
Looking ahead, policy is re -emerging as a major driver. The Com-
mission’s July proposal for the post -2030 EU ETS would slow the
contraction of the emissions cap, extend conditional free alloca-
tion and ease the operation of the Market Stability Reserve. The
measures would leave more allowances in circulation than under
the present framework, easing concerns about future supply con-
straints. The initial market response was positive, however, this is
only the starting point for further negotiations, leaving scope for
revision.
Beyond the EU ETS reform, the proposed linkage with the UK ETS
remains an open issue. A summit expected to advance negotia-
tions in July was postponed following the change in UK leader-
ship, leaving the timetable uncertain. Progress towards linkage
should narrow the spread between UKAs and EUAs as UK allow-
ance prices move closer to EU levels. Once implemented, the link-
age could become a bearish factor for EUA prices by expanding
the pool of available allowances, although its impact would de-
pend on supply conditions across both systems.
Concluding, the EUA outlook for the remainder of 2026 will de-
pend largely on developments across the European energy com-
plex. Geopolitical uncertainty, disruption to Middle Eastern LNG
flows and Europe’s efforts to replenish low gas storage levels will
shape gas and power prices, with changes in fuel -switching eco-
nomics feeding through to carbon. In the near term, compliance

Crude tanker spot markets eased overall this week, with Su-
ezmaxes suffering the largest losses while VLCCs posted modest
gains. The BDTI averaged 2,855, down 3% w-o-w.
Within the VLCC segment, regional performance was mixed. The
Middle East market remained stable, supported by the growing
use of AIS -dark transits through Hormuz, followed by STS trans-
fers off Fujairah or Sohar. Conditions stayed healthy, with steady
enquiry and balanced tonnage availability. West Africa spot rates
retreated w -o-w despite limited tonnage, as demand faded pro-
gressively through the week. The US Gulf opened firmly, carrying
forward the previous week ’s momentum, but a series of failed
fixtures pulled rates lower and weighed on sentiment. Meanwhile,
owners sought longer -period employment for their tonnage.
VLCC TCE rates averaged $334,066/day, up 3% w-o-w.
The expected retreat following the elevated rates of previous
weeks materialized for Suezmaxes, shifting negotiating power
towards charterers. Rates corrected sharply in the Americas,
Black Sea and West Africa as demand and fixing activity weak-
ened, leaving ample tonnage chasing limited cargoes. In the Black
Sea, some owners avoided the region in search of safer and more
economically attractive employment, while at USG, Suezmaxes
lost cargoes to more competitive Aframaxes. MEG remained
broadly stable. Average Suezmax TCE earnings fell 34% w -o-w to
$184,914/day.
The Aframax segment also moved lower, mainly due to subdued
conditions at USG.

The dry bulk market strengthened last week, with broad -based
gains across all segments, led by Capesizes. The BDI averaged
3,031, up 7.5% w-o-w.
Capesizes recorded the sharpest increase, with both the Atlantic
and Pacific basins advancing. In the Pacific, steady miner cargoes
underpinned activity. The Atlantic provided the stronger impetus,
as fresh cargo volumes tightened the market and lifted rates,
supported by enquiries from West Africa and South Brazil. De-
mand moderated towards the end of the week, but a limited pool
of available units maintained upward pressure on rates, kept
owners in a strong position and sustained firm market sentiment.
The Panamax/Kamsarmax market also advanced, supported by a
broad rise in cargo demand rather than any single regional driver.
In the Pacific, North Pacific grain volumes increased as the new
harvest entered export channels, while Australian mineral ship-
ments provided support and typhoon -related delays constrained
vessel supply.

firmer transatlantic cargoes and robust South American demand.
Momentum may ease after recent gains, but limited tonnage
should sustain owners’ leverage.
The Supramax segment was broadly stable last week, with only
minor rate movements amid subdued activity across several re-
gions. In the Pacific, tonnage was absorbed by increased NoPac
grain enquiries, stabilizing rates. Atlantic sentiment improved as
stronger US Gulf activity attracted units, although North America
remained quiet. In Mediterranean, conditions weakened affected
by scarce Black Sea grain shipments, while in Asia, Indonesian
cargoes to the Subcontinent thinned prompt tonnage list.
The Handysize market posted modest gains, led by firm funda-
mentals in the US Gulf, amid robust demand and limited vessel
availability. East Coast South America provided another area of
strength amid increased enquiries. In Asia, healthy demand grad-
ually reduced the tonnage pool, lending further support. South
Atlantic witnessed a gradual weakening of activity.

Ship recycling markets remain broadly healthy, but a shortage
of available tonnage continues to constrain activity. Recyclers
retain a strong appetite, yet robust freight rates across several
vessel classes are leading owners to defer scrapping decisions
and take advantage of the favorable market conditions. The
supply outlook should improve as vessels age and freight mar-
kets normalize, prompting a larger flow of recycling candidates.
At Alang, the market remained stable, with recyclers actively
seeking available candidates and focusing on niche units. This
focus continues to sustain activity amid a shortage of main-
stream tonnage, while India remains less competitive than its
subcontinent rivals but is trying to build on its compliance ad-
vantage, since most of the sector is HKC -certified. Firmer do-
mestic steel prices and a partial recovery in the rupee are also
improving market fundamentals and sentiment.

candidates and weak conditions in the local steel market, where
tepid demand for finished products has left mills reluctant buy-
ers. Sentiment was further weighed down by a weakening of
local currency, with inflationary pressure from elevated energy
costs adding to the strain. Buying appetite remains in place,
though it seems that a meaningful influx of fresh tonnage is
needed before activity can lift.

WEEKLY MARKET REPORT
WEEK 36 · September 4th, 2026
MARKET OVERVIEW
A sharp re-escalation in Middle Eastern geopolitical volatility as a fresh wave of military strikes has
reignited direct conflict along the Persian Gulf, reversing weeks of relative stability. Following locali sed
strikes against coastal installations, security forces targeted two commercial vessels under a newly
implemented reciprocal deterrence policy after outbound crude carriers were struck by airborne
projectiles. In immediate retaliation, missile and drone salvos were launched toward regional staging hubs
hosting international forces across neighbouring territories. This rapid return to open hostilities has
abruptly curtailed hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough, driving global crude futures to multi -week highs
with international benchmarks crossing US$95 a barrel. With worldwide commercial stockpiles and
strategic reserves heavily depleted after months of ongoing disruption, energy markets are factoring in a
renewed structural risk premium, even as downstream domestic refiners run at extraordinary utilisation
rates to capture soaring fuel margins.
Despite the heightened security risks, significant energy volumes continue to move through the corridor
via tightly managed operations. Official monitoring reports indicate that seaborne outflows from the Strait
of Hormuz are averaging roughly 8 million barrels per day, bolstered by an estimated 5 million daily
barrels moving through regional pipeline bypasses. While international naval escorts have shepherded
dozens of laden tankers across the chokepoint to maintain supply continuity to primary Asian consumers,
local defence officials have asserted that the waterway remains under strict surveillance. F leet operators
continue to exercise extreme caution, noting that while physical volumes are escaping through
specialised shuttle arrangements and transponder manipulations, the threat of drone attacks, drifting sea
mines, and localised interdictions keeps maritime insurance rates and spot tanker fixtures elevated.
Broader shifts in energy diplomacy are redrawing trade routes across the Western Hemisphere. A
deepened bilateral agreement granting substantial operational stakes and preferential crude purchasing
rights in Venezuelan oil fields to North American interests is reshaping Latin American flows.

Broader shifts in energy diplomacy are redrawing trade routes across the Western Hemisphere. A

rights in Venezuelan oil fields to North American interests is reshaping Latin American flows. This
reorientation directly impacts long-standing transpacific trade patterns, where East Asian buyers
previously absorbed most local heavy crude exports to settle historical loan facilities. While existing
commercial entanglements ensure that major Asian entities remain embedded across South American
infrastructure, the loss of discounted heavy crude access has forced independent regional refiners to seek
costlier alternatives from Atlantic and northern suppliers. As Western security policies increasingly
emphasise regional economic alignment, participants are anticipating long-term structural changes in
tanker routing and commodity credit settlements across the Pacific basin .

DRY BULK | BDI: 3,628 ▲13.87% (w-o-w)
Dry bulk sector demonstrated notable strength heading into early September, advancing on broad- based
cargo demand and localised fleet bottlenecks even as wider geopolitical disruptions continue to
challenge international trade corridors. Lingering instability in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov has severely
restricted regional agricultural outflows—with monthly wheat shipments dropping to under 2.5 million tons
compared to 6.3 million tons during the same period last year—while the ongoing closure of the Strait of
Hormuz has stalled roughly a quarter of global fertiliser trade and left around 120 to 150 bulk carriers
immobilised.
Despite these headwinds, BDI surged 13.87% end week to reach 3,628 points, and stands as the highest
level seen since December 2023. This upward momentum was spearheaded by the Capesize segment,

Despite these headwinds, BDI surged 13.87% end week to reach 3,628 points, and stands as the highest

where the Capesize index jumped 20.4% to 6,427 points—as aggressive chartering from the three major
mining houses in Australia-to-China routes alongside tight vessel supply in the Atlantic basin. Medium
and smaller bulkers participated fully in the rally; the Panamax index extended its positive run into an
eighth consecutive session by climbing to 2,448 points, supported by a domestic accident in China that
prompted immediate interest in seaborne coking coal, while the Supramax index edged up to 1,67 5 points.
Segment Highlights
Capesize: Capesize surged this week as C5 West Australia-China fixtures pushing into the mid-US$16s on
active miner bookings and typhoon-related port delays in eastern China. Solid import demand amid low
Chinese port stockpiles and tight prompt vessel availability supported the rally across both basins, lifting
T/A earnings to US$55,050’s and Pacific R/V to US$52,150’s per day. However, market sentiment remains
cautious heading into late September laycans, as an influx of ballasters toward Brazil and the clearing of
Chinese port bottlenecks threaten to ease near-term supply tightness against limited fresh demand.
Panamax / Kamsarmax: Panamax firmed steadily across both basins this week, supported by early vessel
bookings for upcoming grain bookings despite current export dips, while a drop in Pacific ballasters and
tightening prompt tonnage left charterers chasing owners' ideas. Although sluggish coal demand and low
river water levels in Kalimantan restricted Indonesian coal flows, replenished Atlantic cargo book helped
underpin positive forward sentiment. Spot returns pushed higher across key Atlantic routes, lifting Brazil
R/V to US$22,100’s and F/H trips to US$30,950’s per day.

persistent softness across the Mediterranean. Spot earnings reflected these mixed market dynamics, with
T/A rates advancing to US$16,950’s while Inter-Pacific runs eased slightly to US$16,400’s per day.

Ongoing Houthi threats in the southern Red Sea have further rattled commercial charterers, eroding the
kingdom's primary workaround. Loadings from the western port of Yanbu, slipped to 3.7 million in July and

Meanwhile, Persian Gulf terminal flows that had rebounded slightly to 800,000 BPD  in July receded once

and renewed exchanges between Washington and Tehran roiling sentiment, benchmark crude in London
climbed back above US$95 per barrel, reviving broader concerns over sustained global inflation.
Segment Highlights
VLCC: MEG saw rates climb as rising Asian exports drove strong chartering demand for Basrah-to-Fujairah
STS shuttle operations, while heightened security risks and recent tanker strikes split the fleet. MEG/China
closed the week at WS678, while in the Atlantic 260,000mt WAFR/China ended on a high ending at WS236.
Suezmax: West African market saw rates gain slightly with trips to UKC closing at WS214, while an
accumulating Atlantic tonnage overhang sapped owners' leverage. In the Black Sea, rates took a tumble
with CPC/Augusta falling 100 points to WS285.
Aframax: Middle East rates saw slight gains as steady early-September crude, along with spillover
demand from a firm VLCC market, allowed owners to leverage tight regional vessel supply. T he
Mediterranean market faces softness this week, as a late-week stall rebuilt prompt tonnage lists, giving
charterers enough leverage to push rates downward as Ceyhan/Lavera ended the week at WS222.
LR1 / LR2: Middle East LR2 saw freight rates flat, as tight vessel supply and earlier tonnage shifts into dirty
trades. TC1 ended the week at around WS565 mark. In the LR1, slight gains were seen, with TC5 trips to
Japan closing at WS621.

CONTAINERS
The container market sustained its upward momentum as upward pressure was led primarily by
transpacific corridors, where spot rates to the U.S. East Coast climbed to surpass the US $10,000 per FEU
threshold, insulated by resilient American cargo volumes and imminent Panama Canal transit slot cuts
starting in September. Effective capacity has been sharply restricted across East Asia, where severe
typhoon disruptions triggered unprecedented operational delays.
According to Sea-Intelligence, schedule reliability across all 14 of Asia’s premier container gateways
declined dramatically; with Shanghai recording its worst performance in 14 years, with on time reliability
dropping 19.2%vto 21%, Ningbo fell 20.1% to 34.6%, and Singapore dipped to 43.2%, as cascading vessel
turnaround delays crippled subsequent voyages.

government infrastructure outlays, and resilient services. While manufacturing purchasing activity saw a
mild seasonal moderation in August, headline industrial confidence remains steady as input cost inflation
recedes to multi-month lows.

minimal change from preceding weeks. Operational tempo across the beaches remained somewhat
subdued as buyers focused on cutting previously delivered inventory, while the complete absence of fresh
market sales left yards without immediate price direction. While fundamental buying appetite is still
present, sentiment lacks forceful conviction amid quiet downstream steel demand, ongoing currency
softness, and high industrial power costs that continue to squeeze operational margins.

any sudden upward momentum in headline vessel price indications.

logistical and currency pressures continued to restrain broad buying appetite across regional mills.
Bangladesh: Import values held firm, underpinned by robust domestic scrap prices hovering at BDT
54,000-55,000/t. US bulk offers remained steady near US$390/t CFR, though escalating global freight rates
prevented major mills from translating active inquiries into firm bookings. Meanwhile, Japanese H2 offers
stood above US$385/t CFR, though softer domestic pricing in Japan is expected to exert downward
pressure shortly.
Turkiye: Deep-sea import benchmarks climbed day-on-day on 2 September, driven by higher rebar
valuations and healthier mill margins. Bullish sellers targeted US$386/t CFR for US material and US$380/t
CFR for EU cargoes, with Baltic-origin expectations rising to US$381-382/t CFR. Strong market sentiment
suggests US-origin HMS 80:20 could challenge US$385-386/t CFR shortly and potentially approach

Concurrently, copper futures consolidated near US$6.57 per pound on Friday as extensive physical
bottlenecks continued to tighten global availability, highlighted by an export embargo from the
Democratic Republic of Congo, a 9.4% year-on-year contraction in Chile’s July output from harsh weather
and repairs, and a 3% dip in China's June refined metal volume to 1.1 million tons. Meanwhile, the global
energy complex saw thermal coal advance to roughly US$145 per ton, touching an eleven-week peak as
persistent Middle Eastern tensions and constrained liquefied natural gas shipments reinforced fuel -
switching needs; and although solar installations in China recently overtook coal capacity for the first time,
coal remains the cornerstone of global baseload power, generating nearly 11,000 TWh in 2026 and
expected by the International Energy Agency to preserve its leading power generation role through 2030.
